[245] The further modernization of the Armed Forces in the period 2005–2008. Recommendation from the Ministry of Defence of 12 March 2004, approved by the Cabinet on the same day

[246] Bondevik II Government

[247] The Armed Forces in transition

[248] status and the way forward

[249] Since mid-2001, the Armed Forces have carried out one of the most extensive restructurings in the history of the Norwegian public sector

[250] The restructuring has so far been successful and has largely gone according to plan

[251] Because the answer lies in emerging from the serious crisis that formed the background for the previous long-term plan

[252] There has been a significant shift in resource flow from support activities to operational activities

[253] The operational national preparedness has been strengthened

[254] Our force contributions in international operations are considered relevant

[255] is of high quality and meets the requirements of modern military operations

[256] This has given Norway great recognition, and strengthened our credibility as a serious contributor and alliance partner

[257] The latter was clearly expressed when NATO moved its Joint Warfare Centre (JWC), which will be central to the work of modernising the alliance's military forces, to Norway

[258] The defense is one of the Norwegian political authorities' most important instruments for securing and promoting national interests, sovereignty and territorial integrity

[259] Norwegian security is inextricably linked to international security

[260] For Norway, stability is therefore an international legal order based on the principles of the UN Charter and the binding alliance agreement

[261] The work in NATO is of paramount importance

[262] An active international role helps safeguard fundamental national interests

[263] At the same time, we must be able to defend our interests and obligations in our own immediate areas, not least in the High North

[264] Security policy developments are accelerating, and the risk picture we face is varied, unpredictable and unclear

[265] At the same time, technological development is proceeding very rapidly

[266] In order for the Armed Forces to be able to contribute to safeguarding Norway's interests and obligations, it must continuously adapt to these ever-changing strategic framework conditions

[267] If this is to be achieved, the ability for military transformation must be central

[268] The Armed Forces must be a learning, living and leading organization, which can deliver what is expected, when it is expected and where it is expected

[269] This is necessary both to be able to handle potential challenges in Norwegian areas on our own, and to be able to contribute to international operations and fulfill our alliance obligations in NATO

[270] The framework conditions for the Armed Forces are constantly changing

[271] As a result, the Armed Forces still face major challenges

[272] The modernization will therefore continue also in the period

[273] No. 42 2003–

[274] The further modernization of the Armed Forces in the period 2005–

[275] In recent years, there has been broad agreement in the Storting on the security and defense policy framework for the Armed Forces' activities

[276] This proposal builds on this agreement

[277] In addition, it is largely based on the recommendations in the Chief of Defence's Military Technical Report 2003 (FSJ MFU

[278] On this comprehensive basis, specific frameworks and proposals are recommended for the further restructuring of the Armed Forces in the period

[279] Status of the restructuring

[280] The goals for the restructuring in the period

[281] This proposition's proposals for new changes in the operational structure and in the logistics and support structure, cf. chapters 5 and 7, establish new transformation goals for the period

[282] These are described in more detail in Chapter

[283] The Storting has given its approval for the government to promote this long-term plan in 2004, even though the current long-term plan is valid

[284] In the context of the need to further strengthen the Armed Forces' operational capability and streamline logistics and support activities, it is therefore appropriate to advance the period by one year, so that this proposition will be valid from 2005 to

[285] This means that a number of efficiency measures can be implemented more quickly than otherwise, and it can be avoided to an even greater extent that resources are spent unnecessarily on parts of the Armed Forces that will eventually be phased out

[286] The following provides an account of the status and forecasts for the ongoing restructuring as of January 2004, based on the existing goals for the restructuring

[287] Main goals for the restructuring of the Armed Forces

[288] The adopted changes in the Armed Forces' organization shall be implemented as soon as possible and no later than December

[289] All activities must have ceased by this date at the units that have been decided to be closed down, and new units must be fully operational

[290] The main economic-administrative goals for the ongoing restructuring are that

[291] – The Armed Forces' operating expenses shall be reduced by a minimum of NOK 2 billion per year, compared to an alternative without the adopted restructuring

[292] – The number of man-years in the Armed Forces must be reduced by a minimum of 5,000 compared to the number as of September

[293] – The extent of the building stock must be reduced by a minimum of 2 million square meters

[294] Property, buildings and equipment that are not to be used in the new structure shall be phased out and, to the greatest extent possible, disposed of, based on market value in accordance with the disposal instructions

[295] The restructuring has strengthened the Armed Forces' operational capability, and has contributed to the Armed Forces being able to respond more quickly with relevant and effective military units in order to solve prioritized tasks

[296] This is of great importance, both in order to be able to address future security challenges in our own immediate vicinity, and in order to be able to fulfill our international obligations

[297] The forces Norway provides for a wide range of operations abroad, have carried out their missions very well, and have shown in practice that the restructuring is effective

[298] The most central economic-administrative goals for the restructuring in the period 2002–2005 appear to be achievable

[299] In broad terms, the interim target for 2003 within the operating area has been achieved, with a reduction of NOK 1.235 million compared to an alternative without restructuring

[300] In 2004, operating savings of approximately NOK 1.9 billion are planned compared to an alternative without restructuring

[301] The main objective for

[302] is fixed, an operating saving of at least NOK 2 billion compared to an alternative without restructuring

[303] The plan to reduce the building stock by 2 million sq m during the period is being followed

[304] As of January 2004, the building stock has been reduced by nearly 1.3 million square meters

[305] The remaining 700,000 sq. m will be taken out in 2004 and 2005. However, challenges remain related to staff reductions, which are an important means of achieving the goals of the restructuring

[306] This area will therefore be prioritized both in 2004 and in the period

[307] As of January 2004, the Armed Forces have achieved a net reduction of approximately 2,000 man-years

[308] Active efforts are being made to implement new measures, and the remaining part of the reduction of 5,000 man-years will be implemented in

[309] The reorganization of the Norwegian Armed Forces Logistics Organization (FLO) is an important tool for reducing the number of man-years

[311] Changes in structure and organization 2002–

[312] The adopted restructuring is on track with regard to the implementation of adopted changes in the structure and organization of the Armed Forces

[313] The exception is the adjustments in the 2003–

[314] The further modernization of the Armed Forces in the period 2005–2008 is reflected in the implementation of material investments that the government explained in St.prop

[315] No

[316] Significant changes have been made to the Armed Forces' top leadership, the command structure, the branches of defense and the Home Guard, as well as to the support functions and civilian agencies

[317] The integrated Ministry of Defence and the Defence Staff have been established, and the experiences from this process have been positive so far

[318] In addition, a new national command structure has been established through the establishment of a joint operational headquarters (FOHK) in Stavanger, with the Regional Command Southern Norway (LDKS) in Trondheim and the Regional Command Northern Norway (LDKN) in Bodø

[319] NATO's new Joint Warfare Centre (JWC) has been established in Stavanger

[320] The center will be the European "footprint" for NATO's Strategic Command Transformation in Norfolk (Virginia, USA), and will ensure that NATO's forces are modernized sufficiently to be able to solve the missions that NATO's operational command (Allied Command Operations – ACO in Belgium) is assigned to solve

[321] Allied training and experience-based learning from completed operations are an important part of this

[322] The branches of defense and the Home Guard have implemented extensive restructuring in their organizations

[323] The reorganization of the operational structure is largely complete, but material investments remain to provide the structure with the necessary quality and operational capability

[324] Through the establishment of the Armed Forces' task forces, the Norwegian Defence Force has acquired qualitatively very good, faster-acting and deployable units

[325] This has made it possible to have a broader involvement in international operations than ever before

[326] However, the number of personnel serving abroad is not higher than before

[327] What is new is that the Army, Navy and Air Force units are able to share tasks by rotation

[328] The ability to react quickly and act quickly was most recently demonstrated by our contribution of a guard and security company to the international security force in Afghanistan, where the main force was in place less than three weeks after the government's decision was made

[329] This was possible at the same time that Norway already had a broad commitment with substantial force contributions, including in Kosovo, the Mediterranean and Iraq, in addition to the fact that there were already force contributions in place in Afghanistan

[330] During the current restructuring period, the Armed Forces' operational management, the Conscription Service, the security service and several school departments have been reorganized, and several joint institutions and departments have been closed down

[331] Several departments have also been established, including two new education and competence centers

[332] Military Medical Education and Competence Center (MUKS) and a joint education and competence center for Air Defense (FLVUKS

[333] The Army's peacekeeping organization has been made more efficient by closing down a number of departments and camps, and by establishing three new education and competence centers

[334] a) an education and competence center for the Army's combat weapons (KAMPUKS), b) an education and competence center for the Army's training weapons (LOGUKS) and c) an education and competence center for the Army's communications (SBUKS

[335] For the response task force

[336] Army (FIST-H) is established as an integral part of Brigade

[337] The 6th Division has been disbanded as a territorial regiment and a reorganized 6th Division Command has been established, so that we are still able to lead an allied division, but do not field the entire division ourselves

[338] In the Navy, the district organization with naval stations has been closed down, and new departments have been established

[339] The school sector has also undergone changes, with all school activities being brought together under the newly established Naval Schools

[340] The Air Force has introduced a new organizational structure at the Air Force's air stations, and a mobile and modular air combat concept has been established in which the air stations no longer have as central a role as previously as independent combat organizations

[341] The air stations are organized into a mobile operational unit and a static support unit

[342] The Norwegian Air Force's Education and Competence Centre (LUKS) has been established as an umbrella organisation, bringing together the inspectorates and their subordinate technical schools

[343] In the Home Guard, the Home Guard districts have taken over the territorial and geographical responsibility that previously lay under the Army regiments

[344] Education in the Home Guard has been reorganized, with the main part of the officer and crew training moved to Værnes

[345] To achieve the efficiency goals for the Armed Forces' restructuring, the organizational changes made in the Armed Forces Logistics Organization (FLO) from 2004 onwards will be crucial

[346] The changes mean that FLO will now become a more efficient, customer-adapted and customer-financed organization, with the other parts of the Armed Forces as the primary customer

[347] Also, streamlining operations at Forsvarsbygg will be of key importance with the aim of reducing both operating and investment costs associated with property, buildings and facilities

[348] Remaining challenges 2002–

[349] Much has been achieved, but there are still challenges related to achieving the full effect of the restructuring

[350] No. 42 2003–

[351] The further modernization of the Armed Forces in the period 2005–

[352] The work to specify and realise the remaining parts of the operating savings target of NOK 2 billion in 2005 is primarily aimed at streamlining operations in the logistics and support structure

[353] This will be followed up in light of the Storting's consideration of the Recommendation

[354] S. no. 93 (2003–2004), cf. St.prp

[355] no. 12 (2003–2004), and is reinforced through a number of additional measures proposed in this proposal

[356] This applies in particular to FFI, and the implementation of the Golf program with a common integrated management system for management and control of personnel, material and financial functions

[357] The introduction of new information technology shall be adapted to existing systems and expertise where this is cost-effective, and shall be based on the assumption that a common management system for the Armed Forces shall be created

[358] Efficiency will be absolutely necessary to be able to make further savings in operations and ensure further reductions in personnel

[359] Personnel are the Armed Forces' most important resource, but at the same time the most cost-driving factor within the defense budget

[360] It is therefore crucial to successfully control the growth of these expenses

[361] Targeted work is being done on measures aimed at excess personnel

[362] These measures are described in more detail in Chapter

[363] In addition, it is even more important to re-prioritize resources from support activities to operational activities

[364] A number of projects are being implemented in this regard, and as the restructuring continues, these challenges will receive great attention

[365] The background to the further restructuring of the Norwegian Armed Forces 2005–

[366] The changes in the structure and activities of the Armed Forces have been significant, but the changes in our environment and in the Armed Forces' external framework conditions have been even greater

[367] It takes time to get rid of the legacy of yesterday's threat image

[368] The residual threat after the Cold War helped to shape parts of our own defense thinking, structure and activities for a long time into the 1990s, despite the fact that the framework conditions were changing rapidly

[369] Through the restructuring of recent years, this has changed, and the threat landscape and assumptions of this era have largely been abandoned

[370] However, aspects of defense thinking, as well as parts of the design of the Armed Forces, are still characterized by the tension between the old and the new

[371] However, tomorrow's challenges cannot be met with yesterday's solutions

[372] The new must therefore be given further priority in the period

[373] The restructuring must continue for two main reasons

[374] The first and most important reason is that strategic frameworks and trends that influence the organisation of the Armed Forces are constantly developing and changing

[375] The second reason is found in national economic conditions, which primarily affect the size of the Defence Force and the strategies and priorities that are necessary to create a modern and flexible defence

[376] Strategic framework conditions

[377] Our security policy environment is dynamic and constantly changing

[378] We face a wide range of possible risks and threats

[379] The threat from international terrorism is one example of cross-border security challenges, and a key framework factor for the further development of the Armed Forces

[380] Technological developments, especially within information and communication technology, will affect the alignment and organization of the Armed Forces

[381] The way the Armed Forces' departments and units operate and are managed will change in the future as a result of this

[382] The opportunities for increased efficiency consist primarily of more effective and precise weapons as well as improved ability to collect and distribute information quickly, both across branches of defense and between strategic and tactical levels

[383] Such technology is also necessary to meet society's expectations that military operations should spare the civilian population and civilian targets to the greatest extent possible, as well as to protect one's own forces in the best possible way

[384] On the other hand, the availability of increasingly advanced technology, as well as society's dependence on technology, creates new vulnerabilities and challenges

[385] Cross-border challenges require closer and increased levels of international cooperation

[386] International security and defense policy cooperation arrangements are characterized by dynamic development and change

[387] In this situation, it is of paramount importance for Norway to support and contribute to continuing cooperation within the UN, and to strengthening and maintaining the international legal order

[388] At the same time, the NATO dimension and international defense policy cooperation constitute a central framework for our security and the development of the Armed Forces

[389] Only through close international cooperation and an increased focus on multinational solutions together with allies can we maintain a modern defense, both in terms of expertise, technology and resource use

[390] The changes in the security landscape and in strategic conditions in general mean changed tasks for the Armed Forces

[391] The armed forces have been given more and more complex tasks in the borderland between war and peace, and in 2003–2004 the St.prop

[392] No. 42 The further modernization of the Armed Forces in the period 2005–2008 between military and civilian activities

[393] We cannot therefore, in the same way as before, base the Defence's operational planning on assumptions about where, when and in what form future challenges may arise

[394] The threat from international terrorism has shown how little relevant such traditional mobilization plans are

[395] New tasks do not require a scaled-down version of the old Armed Forces, but a new type of defense

[396] What we need now is the ability to respond quickly with relevant military units

[397] This is particularly important for the Armed Forces' ability to independently carry out its tasks in Norwegian areas, because national crises and episodes of limited scope could arise very quickly and would have to be handled by Norway alone

[398] Internationally, we will always operate together with others, and we will therefore be able to choose to a greater extent when and with what we want to contribute

[399] We are unlikely to have such freedom of choice with regard to challenges in our local areas

[400] The Armed Forces' ability to be flexible and react quickly with relevant units will therefore be particularly important for Norway's ability to safeguard the exercise of national authority, assert sovereignty and manage crises

[401] Further modernization of the Armed Forces is therefore crucial for our national security

[402] The above-mentioned developments necessitate a continuation of the transformation towards a flexible, high-quality defence

[403] This flexibility means, firstly, that the Armed Forces must be developed with the aim of being relevant to the sum of the prioritized tasks

[404] The same forces must be able to handle the entire spectrum of the Armed Forces' prioritized tasks, regardless of whether these are to be solved alone or together with others, nationally or internationally

[405] Secondly, it implies that the Armed response must be made more adaptable, so that it can be continuously adapted to the prevailing strategic environment

[406] Only in this way can the Armed Forces remain a relevant security policy instrument

[407] In the work to create a flexible defense, transformation is a key word

[408] Transformation means conversion or qualitative change

[409] Transformation is a continuous and proactive process, in which innovative concepts, doctrines and capabilities are developed and integrated to improve and/or make the Armed Forces more efficient, including improving its ability to operate together with its own and other forces

[410] It is based on the premise that modern technology enables new and more effective forms of operation, organization and management in the new security landscape

[411] Transformation emphasizes creativity, innovation and adaptability

[412] Establishing the ability for transformation throughout the Armed Forces will be central in the period

[413] –2008. If we are to succeed in creating the defense we want, changes in the personnel area are crucial, because the new defense has different needs in this field than the old one

[414] This applies both to the age and rank structure of the commanding corps and to the personnel's competence, level of experience and the Armed Forces' command capabilities

[415] A flexible defense, where the entire structure must be able to quickly complete its tasks at home and abroad, places different demands on the personnel composition than a defense that must primarily be able to meet a conventional military invasion of Norwegian territory through the mobilization of large parts of the population

[416] Modern technology and complex operations require an increased level of specialized expertise in the Armed Forces, especially at the lower levels of the Armed Forces organization

[417] Changes in the personnel area are thus one of the most important structural measures to lay the foundation for a more flexible defense

[418] New measures in this regard are therefore discussed in detail in this proposal

[561] Norwegian security policy in a new era

[562] Security in a globalized world: Norway's security policy situation is characterized by a broader and more complex risk picture, in which a comprehensive existential threat has been replaced by uncertainty and unpredictability with regard to the security challenges we may face

[563] This also applies to potential security challenges in Norway's own immediate areas, where the strategic importance of the High North and resource management in large ocean areas will continue to constitute key framework conditions for Norwegian security and defense policy

[564] Our time is characterized by increased globalization

[565] Overall, the effects of globalization are predominantly positive

[566] It has created new opportunities and contributed to important advances, technologically, economically, politically and culturally

[567] International cooperation has been strengthened as a result of the world's nations seeing this as best serving their interests, as a response to the need to solve problems together

[568] At the same time, globalization has also brought with it a number of new challenges and issues

[569] Balancing involves, among other things, extensive interdependence between countries and regions, with a reduced significance of geographical distance and extensive changes in the relationships within and between states and societies as a result

[570] The challenges for Norwegian and international security have changed to a large extent as a result of this

[571] The international community's work for peace and security aims to resolve conflicts in ways other than through the use of force, primarily through the use of the UN and in line with international law

[572] This approach is a pillar of the government's foreign and security policy, in which the UN is the most important global cooperation body

[573] Despite this work, however, the armed forces have

[574] Conflict and war significantly left their mark on the international situation after the end of the Cold War

[575] Armed conflicts within states and the use of violence by non-state actors also create new security challenges

[576] The consequences of these will increasingly affect the international community and threaten international development, peace and security

[577] The traditional perception of the purpose of security policy has been linked to the defense of state power and its fundamental interests – state security

[578] State security is a fundamental security need that, when the state is faced with an existential threat, can legitimize the use of all its available resources

[579] State security can also be challenged through political and military pressure against Norwegian authorities or through more limited attacks against Norwegian authorities and interests

[580] New security challenges and new types of armed conflicts after the end of the Cold War have led to increased emphasis on societal security

[581] Civil security is about safeguarding the safety of the civilian population and securing central societal functions and important infrastructure against attack and other damage in situations where the existence of the state as such is not threatened

[582] At the same time, developments have led to an increased focus on human security, which is an important part of societal security and concerns the protection of individual rights, where human rights and, not least, the right to life and personal security are at the center

[583] There is a close connection and smooth transitions between these security dimensions, and it is difficult to draw clear distinctions

[584] These cannot therefore be considered an attempt at a strictly defined and exhaustive categorization of the concept of security, but rather as an aid and illustration to describe the changes in the risk picture and the need for a changed focus in security and defense policy

[585] Here, new threats to societal security and more limited threats to state security are today more likely than the danger of more traditional extensive military attacks against Norway

[586] The broader understanding of the concept of security that is used as a basis has great significance for the tasks that military forces can be assigned to, and therefore also for the Armed Forces' training, equipment and operational concepts

[587] The prevailing security strategy in the Western world today places increased emphasis on collective security, both in a global and regional framework

[588] Security is not something that each state can ensure on an individual basis or with unilateral emphasis

[589] No. 42 2003–

[590] The further modernization of the Armed Forces in the period 2005–2008 on traditional state security – it must be created and protected in collaboration with others

[591] Cooperation between military and civilian authorities has therefore also gained increased importance in the work of ensuring our common security

[592] Fundamental Norwegian security interests The task of security policy is to safeguard and promote fundamental national security interests

[593] A clear formulation of such interests is therefore important, especially in light of the changing environment and security challenges

[594] Normally, the defense of fundamental national interests will be done with

[595] more effective means than military ones, but as a last resort, and after all other means have been considered, Norway must also be willing to defend them with military force

[596] In addition to state, societal and human security, protecting the welfare, environment and economic security of the Norwegian people are fundamental Norwegian security interests

[597] This is also closely related to control over and proper exploitation and protection of the large resources Norway manages on the continental shelf and in our large ocean areas

[598] These constitute a key prerequisite for value creation in Norway, and are also of strategic importance for other states

[599] This links important Norwegian interests to global developments in the energy sector, to the interests of other states in this area and to the protection of oil and gas installations

[600] The same applies to international rules and principles related to the freedom of the seas and the management of marine resources

[601] Furthermore, certain fundamental values are included as important components among Norway's central security interests

[602] Gross violations of these values ​​can lead to conflicts that develop in such a way that they also have to be handled with military means

[603] Norwegian security interests are therefore affected by challenges that may threaten the international legal order, human rights, democracy, the principles of the rule of law, economic security and the living environment. In other words, Norway's security interests are closely linked to developments in our international surroundings

[604] A fundamental Norwegian security interest is therefore the development of an international legal order that strengthens human rights and peace, stability, security and development, both within a regional and a global framework

[605] Norway's national security cannot be seen in isolation from European security in general, whether politically, legally, economically or militarily

[606] At the same time, developments in Europe's surrounding areas are increasingly affecting European security

[607] Continuing and strengthening transatlantic and European security cooperation, in which active American engagement in Europe continues to be a central element, is crucial for Norwegian security

[608] Furthermore, it is of great importance to Norway that the EU's role in European and international security, including the development of a separate European military capability, is further developed in harmony with NATO's role and transatlantic cooperation, so that the EU and NATO complement each other

[609] This development must promote the overall real capacity for conflict prevention, crisis management and resolution, and promote a more even burden-sharing within the transatlantic community

[610] In a world characterized by globalization, an expansion of the stable security zone in the original North Atlantic area is also becoming increasingly important

[611] For Norway, linking Russia to close and mutual cooperation with its surroundings, including through a strategic partnership with institutions such as NATO and the EU, is of particular importance in this regard

[612] From a global perspective, it is of paramount importance that the UN's ability to handle international crises and conflicts, as well as to contribute to the further development of the international legal order, is strengthened, and that the work of other institutions helps to support the UN's role

[613] Norway's security policy space for action is closely linked to our strategic position

[614] This position is largely determined by a power political structure in which NATO, the USA, the EU and Russia constitute the most important centers of gravity

[615] The relationship between the centers of gravity in this system has changed in recent years

[616] Russia's position has been weakened, while the US and the EU have gained in importance. NATO's role and tasks have also changed

[617] These changes have strengthened Norwegian security in a very fundamental way

[618] As a small state, Norway initially has limited room for manoeuvre

[619] The framework is defined not least by other and larger states

[620] For small states, the multilateral space for action is usually crucial

[621] In multilateral forums such as the UN, NATO and the EU, one seeks to safeguard one's own interests and goals through understanding and cooperation with other states

[622] Multilateral solutions in practice serve to re 2003–2004 St.prop

[623] The further modernization of the Armed Forces in the period 2005–2008 will change how individual states use their national scope for action

[624] International rules and norms are particularly important when it comes to security and conflict prevention

[625] International law is of particular importance here, not least respect for the UN Charter and the principles for maintaining international peace and security

[626] The UN Security Council has a key role in legitimizing measures against states and possibly other actors that threaten peace and security

[627] At the same time, the right to self-defense is directly enshrined in Article 51 of the UN Charter. Article 5 of the Atlantic Charter (collective defense) is based directly on Article 51 of the UN Charter. Norway's ability to safeguard its security interests depends on the government's ability to use the full spectrum of instruments within the security policy space in an optimal manner

[628] The defense sector plays a central role in this context, including in the work of building and maintaining alliances with related countries

[629] However, military means will only be used when other means have not worked, are not applicable or are not relevant

[630] Security policy development trends

[631] Security policy challenges

[632] a new risk picture

[633] A broad and complex risk picture characterizes Norway's security policy environment

[634] The challenges and potential threats are more diffuse than before, and are characterized by smooth transitions between the national and the international, and between peace, crisis, armed conflict and war

[635] Increasing interdependence characterizes relations between countries as well as continents

[636] This helps to blur the distinction between national and international security

[637] Threats can arise and develop quickly and without much warning, partly because non-state actors can also threaten security

[638] The possibility exists that Norway could be drawn into conflicts that we are not initially a party to – both directly and indirectly

[639] Several minor conflicts can occur simultaneously

[640] Major international armed conflicts, including extensive war between states, cannot be discounted either

[641] Contradictions between states and different groups can spread in new and unexpected directions, causing new conflicts

[642] The possibility that we or our allies could be subjected to attacks with weapons of mass destruction is real

[643] The challenges and potential threats we face are more numerous and more complex than before

[644] All of this presents Norway with new challenges and has consequences for the Armed Forces as a security policy instrument

[645] Key global developments

[646] The majority of armed conflicts that have unfolded since the end of the Cold War have taken place between actors within a country's borders

[647] National, political, ethnic, cultural and religious divisions can still create conflicts in a number of places in the world, especially in areas with major social and economic challenges

[648] In the areas surrounding Europe, it is particularly in parts of Asia, the Middle East, the Caucasus and North Africa that the potential for such conflicts is great

[649] This type of conflict has proven to be an international security problem, both because they often have destabilizing consequences regionally, and because they challenge international norms and rules of law

[650] Increased emphasis on human rights has created a new debate related to the issue of "humanitarian intervention

[651] Globalization is characterized in particular by a more integrated world economy

[652] As a result, we are faced with increasing economic interdependence internationally

[653] Overall, the effects of this are positive, with increased trade across borders and an increased standard of living in a number of countries

[654] Many previously developing countries have experienced significant economic growth

[655] In other places, however, development has contributed to undermining traditional social structures

[656] Such contradictory developments can contribute to destabilization, rivalry and conflict between and within states, and in some cases to the disintegration of states and societies

[657] Globalization also encompasses the cultural, ideological, religious, informational and political spheres

[658] Satellite television, the Internet, commercialized mass culture, increased travel and population movements, access to new ideas and new knowledge, as well as a wealth of different products and services, directly intervene in societies that until recently were relatively shielded from such extensive influence

[659] For some states or groups, these changes are not perceived as progress, but as attacks on their own culture, identity and autonomy

[660] This can lead to various types of countermeasures against the actors who are most strongly perceived to be behind globalization

[661] Such countermeasures could include attacks from international terrorism, which often have direct links to international organized crime

[662] Non-state actors have a wide range of tools at their disposal, which in addition to armed attacks can include undermining the legitimacy of local political regimes, blackmail, information attacks, etc

[669] The experiences of recent years show that international terrorism represents a very serious global security challenge

[670] No part of the world or nation can feel safe

[671] Terrorism's inventiveness in attack methods and choice of targets means that we must expect to be surprised by where, when and against whom it strikes

[672] The risk of actions that could cause mass killings and enormous destruction is increasing

[673] International terrorism can only be combated by using several different security policy instruments

[674] These must be used in a holistic manner and across the full range of relevant areas of focus

[675] It is important to protect current terrorist targets so that they are difficult to access

[676] Vulnerabilities in such targets must be addressed, and there is a need to have the ability to effectively limit the extent of damage that may occur

[677] The international community must stand together in the effort to stop terrorists before they cause harm

[678] It is a serious problem that in some states and regions there is little ability to effectively enforce law and order

[679] It is therefore important to prevent areas of lawlessness that could provide an increased breeding ground for international terrorism

[680] At the same time, measures must be implemented to prevent terrorists from gaining access to weapons of mass destruction

[681] Restricting terrorists' access to financial resources, especially from international organized crime, is an important part of this

[682] In a number of countries, there are serious conflicts related to issues of control over limited resources, and where there is a real danger of a collapse of state power

[683] States where the central power no longer has control, or which lack a unified national identity, pose problems, both as hotbeds of international terrorism and in the form of an increased risk of armed conflict, regional destabilization, large refugee flows and humanitarian disasters

[684] The demographic development in parts of the most economically developed parts of the world, with birth rates below the reproduction level, has led to a changed age composition of the population, with a strong growth in the proportion of elderly people

[685] The opposite is the case in many of the economically least developed parts of the world

[686] The result is poorer living conditions for large population groups in a number of countries

[687] In the long term, pressure on the most economically developed parts of the world may increase further as a result of global population growth

[688] The development and spread of technology contributes to economic growth and is an inherent part of globalization

[689] At the same time, today's advanced technology has made modern societies more complex and vulnerable

[690] This represents an increased risk

[691] The spread of modern technology globally also has direct consequences for international military development

[692] Modern military capabilities, including weapons systems with long range and great potential impact, will increasingly be reserved for a limited number of resource-rich countries

[693] The proliferation of missile technology and weapons of mass destruction has been widespread over the past 30 years, despite a targeted policy of non-proliferation and export control

[694] It is a fact that many of the countries that either have or wish to gain access to weapons of mass destruction and their means of delivery have a somewhat strained relationship with international obligations and the values and principles enshrined in the UN Charter and international law

[695] There is a significant risk that the proliferation of missile technology and weapons of mass destruction will continue, despite increased emphasis on non-proliferation and other preventive measures

[696] Non-state actors may also be able to use weapons of mass destruction

[697] While many of the global trends point towards a more unpredictable and chaotic future, extensive integration is underway in large parts of the most economically developed part of the world

[698] For Norway, this development contributes to safe and stable local areas

[699] The expansion of both NATO and the EU, and strengthened cooperation with Russia, will expand and consolidate this stable environment

[700] At the same time, global developments could create new threats to North America and Europe, including Russia

[701] This will again require collective efforts to create control and security

[702] Societal developments and trends of importance to the Armed Forces

[703] A number of trends and developments in society contribute to accentuating and influencing the overall security policy developments described above

[704] The further modernization of the Armed Forces in the period 2005–

[705] In a crisis situation, both at home and abroad, the expectation in civil society will largely be that society will function as normally as possible, while at the same time handling crises, including by using military means

[706] At the same time, modern conflicts rarely take place between well-organized military forces that fight battles on a limited battlefield

[707] This means that the distinction between peace, armed conflict and war has become less clear than before, and, together with other changes and trends in society, means that the framework conditions for the Norwegian Defence's operational activities have radically changed

[708] As described by the Vulnerability Committee (NOU 2000:24), and later followed up in Recommendation

[709] P. no. 9 (2002–

[710] No. 17 (2001–2002), the task of safeguarding societal security is increasingly important given the vulnerability of modern society

[711] Modern society's critical dependence on information and communication technology brings with it new security challenges

[712] Centralization creates vulnerable concentrations of people and resources

[713] The interdependence between different functions of society and in the relationship with the outside world increases the risk of ripple effects from events that may initially be limited or isolated

[714] Military security of supply was previously largely based on requisitions and pre-planned stockpiles of critical goods

[715] The need for such warehouses is greatly diminished, and security of supply is also affected by factors such as ownership in the private sector, reduced importance of inventories in general, and greater focus on continuous deliveries to meet demand

[716] The changing risk picture, as well as the need for comprehensive societal resource utilization, requires close cooperation between the Armed Forces and civilian actors on the supply side, with the aim of making logistics systems sufficiently robust and ensuring the most rational and efficient use of available resources

[717] An example of this is collaboration with the health sector on emergency preparedness and expertise related to important resource areas

[718] However, items that cannot be obtained within an acceptable notice period must still be part of the inventory

[719] In a crisis situation, available resources must meet the needs of civil society

[720] The Armed Forces cannot therefore rely on civil society to support military operations and military activities in all situations

[721] This has implications for the alignment of the Armed Forces' logistics apparatus and civil preparedness

[722] The armed forces' operational departments must bring sufficient supplies to ensure endurance, and the logistics apparatus must have the same mobility and deployability as the forces it supports

[723] In addition, a logistics organization must be established that is capable of resupplying the combat units, to provide sufficient endurance according to national and allied requirements

[724] The need for cooperation between military and civilian actors in crises and conflicts has increased and at the same time changed form

[725] This is a natural consequence of the development in the risk picture outlined earlier

[726] Civil-military cooperation is a concept that spans a very broad field with many different actors, and whose content is largely situational

[727] In some cases, the Armed Forces support civilian activities, while in other situations the Armed Forces are supported by civilian resources

[728] The armed forces should, in a national context and within the framework of available resources, be able to contribute to societal security, for example through support to the police and civil authorities in disasters and crises, and will constitute an important capacity for protecting society against new and unconventional security challenges (cf. also box

[729] The Armed Forces have a wide range of resources at their disposal that can be valuable in crises that may affect civilian society

[730] The objectives of using military force outside Norway will in many cases be to end conflicts, achieve stabilization, and lay the foundation for civilian reconstruction

[731] This cannot be achieved by military platoons alone

[732] Civilian and military actors will operate in the same geographical area, often simultaneously, with parallel activities that interfere with each other

[733] It is therefore necessary for civilian and military actors to coordinate activities, clarify roles and work together towards common goals

[734] However, there may be different perspectives and priorities between non-governmental humanitarian organizations on the one hand, and military actors on the other

[735] The greatest possible degree of cooperation must be achieved based on

[736] on internationally recognized guidelines, as well as knowledge of and respect for each other's roles and functions

[737] Norwegian military forces will primarily be used for military missions

[738] Situations may arise where military missions for limited periods contain elements and purposes of a civilian or humanitarian nature

[739] In such situations, it is crucial that efforts are coordinated with the UN and other civilian actors, to ensure effective achievement of objectives and to avoid ambiguity about the division of roles

[740] Experience has shown that there is a need for a broad set of instruments in connection with peace operations for them to be successful

[741] Military presence is often crucial to ensuring the stability necessary for positive political and economic development

[742] But also police resources, contributions to the development of the judiciary, humanitarian aid and development assistance are important

[743] No. 42 2003–

[744] The further modernization of the Armed Forces in the period 2005–2008 is an element in the work to create lasting peace and reconciliation

[745] The need for cooperation between civilian and military actors affects the Armed Forces' competence needs

[746] Civil-military cooperation will also significantly influence the way operations are conducted

[747] In many situations, effective cooperation and appropriate division of roles will constitute a critical factor for the progress of operations

[748] The media must be expected to play an active and critical role in all future conflicts

[749] The media will report on the progress and consequences of the operations at close range, and will help influence public opinion's perception of the situation in the area where the crisis is unfolding

[750] The international media's focus on conflicts and conflict areas also contributes to increased attention to the humanitarian consequences of conflicts

[751] A critical press is a central part of a democratic society

[752] In modern conflicts, the population is expected to have access to updated information about the situation in general and Norwegian forces in particular

[753] The Armed Forces shall, as far as operational considerations allow, seek to keep the media up to date

[754] In some situations, there will be a tension between the media's desire for openness and the government's need to limit the flow of information, for example to ensure the safety of its own personnel and operations

[755] Armed Forces personnel must have the competence to handle the press and information aspect within the framework of the requirements of the operational activities

[756] The value placed on human security entails a strong desire to avoid the loss of human life, both civilian and military

[757] This has major implications for operational conditions, and places changed demands on the Armed Forces' capacities and expertise

[758] The use of military force must, to the greatest extent possible, avoid unnecessary and unintended harm to civilian communities during operations

[759] Great emphasis must also be placed on protecting our own forces, both in the form of modern equipment and through the way operations are planned and carried out

[760] Modern technology to support the provision of an updated information base, and weapons systems with high precision and effectiveness, are critical capabilities in this context

[761] At the same time, the use of military force must be directed and implemented within the rules of international law, and within politically defined limits and conditions (cf. chapter

[762] Limited conflicts will often require significantly expanded political control, and the actions of individual soldiers in such conflicts can have major consequences

[763] At the same time, it is important that military forces are given the necessary powers and freedom of action so that missions can be carried out effectively without excessive risk

[764] This necessitates high training standards and increased competence to assess complex situations, even at the lower levels of the Armed Forces organization

[765] In short, the Armed Forces' orientation and operational activities must reflect developments in and expectations from civil society, and meet the demands of modern conflicts

[766] This has consequences for competence-related matters as well as for doctrines and concepts, equipment and organization

[767] Overall security policy goals

[768] Norwegian security policy must be designed as part of Norwegian overall policy, and be in line with the values that are prominent in Norwegian society

[769] Here, democracy, human rights, respect for international law and the goal of contributing to international peace and stability are central, with the UN as the most important actor

[770] At the same time, security policy must help safeguard fundamental national security interests related to stability and security in our immediate areas

[771] Norway is a small state with a close community of values ​​and interests with other Western countries

[772] We are geographically located in an area rich in resources, where the neighborhood with Russia remains an important framework factor

[773] The sum of these factors creates a significant degree of continuity regarding the overall conditions for and priorities in Norwegian security policy

[774] The goals of Norwegian security policy form the basis for the application of Norwegian security policy instruments, and contribute to operationalizing Norway's fundamental security interests (cf. Chapter

[775] The security policy developments and framework conditions summarized in the foregoing justify certain adjustments that are based on the adjustment and clarification of the overarching security policy goals that the Storting based on in Recommendation

[776] no. 342 (2000–2001) and Recommendation

[777] P. No. 232 (2001–

[778] It is important to present the security policy goals in a way that better reflects the prevailing security policy challenges, not least the increased emphasis placed on societal security

[779] On this basis, the government proposes that the overall goals for Norwegian security policy for the period 2005–2008 shall be: – to prevent war and the emergence of various threats to Norwegian and collective security; – to contribute to peace, stability and further development of the international legal order; – to safeguard Norwegian sovereignty, Norwegian rights and interests and protect Norwegian freedom of action against political, military and other pressure; – together with our allies to defend Norway and NATO against attacks and threats; – to secure society against attacks and threats from state and non-state actors

[780] The further modernization of the Armed Forces in the period 2005–2008 and interests and protect Norwegian freedom of action against political, military and other pressure; – together with our allies to defend Norway and NATO against attacks and threats; – to secure society against attacks and threats from state and non-state actors

[781] These goals are all of fundamental importance for Norwegian security, and will provide us with a good basis for managing the development and use of Norway's security policy instruments

[782] Here, the Armed Forces will continue to be one of the most central instruments at the disposal of the Norwegian authorities in the future

[783] Security policy focal points and Norway's immediate surroundings

[784] Cooperation within the UN

[785] The UN plays a key role in Norwegian security policy

[786] Norwegian security is closely linked to the existence of well-functioning arrangements for security cooperation in a global framework

[787] The changing risk picture, where geography has become less important and threats are global, helps to further reinforce this point

[788] Cooperation within the framework of the UN, which has the primary responsibility for maintaining international peace and security, is of great importance to Norway

[789] Norway benefits from international security challenges finding solutions within a broad consensus, based on the principles of the UN Charter and through anchoring in international law

[790] Norway places crucial importance on the UN as a global and overarching security policy focal point

[791] In the future, the UN will continue to be the most central arena for coordination and cooperation to meet the security challenges that the world community may face

[792] It is the government's goal that Norway will actively contribute to ensuring that the UN is able to carry out its tasks effectively, including through military contributions to UN operations

[793] The UN has, based on experiences from the 1990s, expanded its concept for peace operations

[794] The UN Expert Panel on Peacekeeping Operations concluded in the Brahimi Report from 2000 that the traditional concept of peacekeeping operations should be expanded, and that the UN needed forces with more robust rules of engagement and the ability to generate deterrence, to prevent the UN from becoming a powerless spectator to human rights violations, ethnic cleansing or violations of agreements

[795] The UN has also decided to follow a number of proposals from the Brahimi report on improving the UN's ability to rapidly deploy and lead peacekeeping operations

[796] The military resources made available to the UN must be developed to tackle a broad spectrum of challenges, have the necessary response capability and be sufficiently robust

[797] The demands placed on the Armed Forces within the NATO framework and with regard to being able to tackle potential security challenges nationally, point in the same direction

[798] The UN itself is not able to carry out all the peace operations that have been necessary to establish in the work for international peace and security

[799] The UN has therefore wanted regional organizations such as the EU and NATO to take on greater responsibility, and in a number of cases the UN has given mandates to operations where member states or regional organizations are responsible for the actual implementation, such as in Iraq, Afghanistan and the Balkans

[800] Through such a division of labor, regional organizations such as NATO and the EU can relieve the UN, thereby strengthening the UN's role and power to act

[801] In this way, the international legal framework is ensured, while the UN must not be directly responsible for operations that the organization does not have the resources, command structure or apparatus to carry out

[802] Operations led by the UN and operations carried out with a UN mandate on behalf of the world organization are therefore not in conflict, quite the opposite

[803] Both parts are about supporting the UN's work for international peace and security

[804] Within the overall framework set by the UN, NATO remains the cornerstone of Norwegian security policy

[805] NATO's purpose is to protect the freedom and security of its member countries by political and military means

[806] This is a guarantee of mutual assistance, where an attack against one is to be considered an attack against all

[807] Today, NATO maintains its function through its ability to meet threats and security challenges where they arise

[808] Furthermore, NATO works actively to promote security and stability throughout the Euro-Atlantic area

[809] NATO truly makes the transatlantic connection that links the security of North America to European security

[810] For Norway, an overarching goal is to actively contribute to NATO being able to carry out its overall security tasks in a credible and effective manner

[811] NATO's use of military force will, in the short and medium term, primarily be linked to crisis management and conflict prevention

[812] There are currently no direct conventional military threats to NATO's area, but international terrorism and the St.prp

[813] No. 42 2003–

[814] The further modernization of the Armed Forces in the period 2005–2008 and the proliferation of weapons of mass destruction and long-range missiles represent a new type of threat to the societies, sovereignty and territorial integrity of the Allies

[815] Active measures against the continued proliferation of weapons of mass destruction, their means of delivery and international terrorism will therefore remain a key Alliance concern

[816] NATO's primary geographical focus is the Euro-Atlantic area, with emphasis on preventing, containing and resolving regional crises and conflicts that could develop into threats to the security of one or more member states

[817] However, the new security challenges have a more global scope

[818] This has had consequences for NATO cooperation

[819] NATO's strategic concept from the spring of 1999 and the decisions at the Prague summit in the autumn of 2002 underline that the Alliance's military forces must undergo major changes to meet a wide range of new tasks and challenges

[820] Credible ability to fulfill the Alliance's tasks requires relevant and rapidly available operational military capabilities that are able to operate effectively together

[821] Not least, European and American forces must be able to operate together

[822] This means that important technological disparities must be sought to be levelled, the technological gap between American and most European military units must be reduced, and that consideration for allied interoperability must be the guiding principle on both sides of the Atlantic

[823] The NATO countries' commitment to transforming their military forces through joint defense planning and the integrated military structure plays a crucial role here

[824] This will also be crucial for the development of the Norwegian Armed Forces, and help strengthen the Armed Forces' ability to ensure Norwegian security

[825] For NATO to have the ability to meet security policy challenges where needed, it is of central importance that NATO countries' military forces are able to act quickly and effectively

[826] In other words, the strengths must be usable and accessible

[827] There is a great need for both forces with rapid reaction ability, and forces that provide endurance over time

[828] The decisions at the Prague summit in the autumn of 2002 help to ensure that NATO has the capabilities needed to meet future challenges, but it is the responsibility of member states to make these forces usable and deployable

[829] Usable forces are characterized by being quickly available for action when needed, and by having the capacity needed

[830] The forces must be of such a standard that no significant training is required to be able to solve the tasks they are assigned, and they must be able to go where the need arises

[831] Usability is achieved through training, exercises and cooperation, and by ensuring that the forces have sufficient logistical support and adapted materiel

[832] NATO's ability to undertake political commitments in the form of military operations can only be safeguarded by increasing the usability of its military forces

[833] The Alliance's ongoing transformation will contribute to this

[834] Security policy developments and developments in NATO mean that it is becoming even more important for Norway to develop close defense policy cooperation with allied countries in order to realize the intentions to develop relevant military capabilities, as decided at the Prague summit

[835] The North Sea Strategy (cf. Box 3.4) will be central in this connection

[836] For Norway and other smaller countries, it is also of fundamental importance to protect and strengthen NATO's consultation mechanisms, among other things to prevent the political marginalization of smaller countries

[837] The principle of consensus is important, but requires flexibility and a willingness to compromise for NATO to function effectively

[838] This requires that even small countries must assume active responsibility

[839] In this context, it is absolutely fundamental that Norway is perceived as a credible ally – both politically and militarily

[840] At the political level, the alliance has undergone significant changes to adapt to the new security policy situation

[841] NATO has adapted to meet a broader range of tasks and challenges, by building on and further developing the common values and interests, and the political and military structures, that made the alliance an effective instrument during the Cold War

[842] This has also meant that the political dimensions of alliance cooperation and NATO's role as a consultation forum have gained a broader scope and increased importance

[843] Furthermore, the extensive expansion of the alliance and the expanded cooperation with various groups of partner countries constitute key features of the development

[844] In 2004, NATO expanded with seven new countries (Bulgaria, Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania, Romania, Slovakia and Slovenia), bringing the total to 26 member states

[845] In parallel, the Alliance has strengthened cooperation with Russia, Ukraine, the remaining partner countries within the framework of the Partnership for Peace, and with the countries participating in NATO's Mediterranean Dialogue

[846] This development is an expression of the inclusive and stabilizing role the alliance wants to play in a new era

[847] The structural changes in NATO are significant and far-reaching, and the main objective is to strengthen the alliance's operational capabilities

[848] In more recent times, the establishment of NATO

[851] Initiative to strengthen NATO's operational capability

[852] Response Force (NRF

[853] The NRF was decided to be established at the NATO summit in Prague in November

[854] A temporary force was established on 15 October

[855] The NRF will become NATO's new rapid reaction force

[856] Participation in the NRF will therefore represent a central alliance commitment and be an important contribution to safeguarding collective security

[857] The NRF shall be the driving factor for the alliance's transformation

[858] Consensus among NATO member states will continue to be a prerequisite for deploying the force in specific operations

[859] Following prior political decisions, the force will be able to carry out a number of different types of missions

[860] The NRF should be able to

[861] – Conduct evacuation operations of affected personnel from various crisis areas

[862] – Support consequence management, for example after attacks with weapons of mass destruction and in humanitarian disasters

[863] – Conduct crisis management operations, including peacekeeping operations

[864] – Support counter-terrorism operations

[865] – Conduct embargo operations

[866] The NRF must also be able to conduct operations that secure a bridgehead for subsequent divisions, including in areas with hostile forces, and be deployed and used to demonstrate military capability for the purpose of supporting diplomatic handling of crisis situations

[867] The NRF will be able to be deployed to carry out missions both within and outside the territories of NATO countries

[868] This means that the NRF will also be available for rapid deployment to handle any crises in Norway and adjacent areas

[869] The plan for the development of the NRF is ambitious, and assumes an initial operational capacity in October 2004, and full operational capacity by October

[870] Only then will it be able to resolve all types of drafts

[871] The NRF is expected to consist of multinational task forces totaling around 20,000 soldiers from all branches of defense

[872] Future deployments of the NRF will be built around the six rapidly deployable corps headquarters (including EURO CORPS) in the NATO force structure and their brigades

[873] The maritime contributions will for the time being be built around NATO's standing maritime forces

[874] Force contributions to the NRF must satisfy very high operational requirements

[875] NATO's new command structure In June 2003, NATO adopted profound changes to the command structure

[876] It is now organized into two separate pillars, each led by a strategic-level headquarters

[877] one to lead operations and one to oversee transformation and competence building

[878] The decision means that NATO's operational chain of command will be streamlined by significantly reducing the number of headquarters

[879] The decision means that the former NATO headquarters in Stavanger has been closed down and replaced with a Joint Warfare Centre (JWC) at the same location, and that NATO's Combined Air Operations Centre (CAOC) at Reitan will be closed down

[880] JWC in Stavanger is subject to Allied Command Transformation (ACT) in the USA

[881] The new headquarters in Stavanger will play a central role in strengthened cooperation to develop relevant and interoperable military capabilities

[882] JWC is responsible for planning and implementing education, training, testing doctrines and developing new concepts

[883] To support this activity, JWC will have two subordinate units

[884] – The Joint Analysis and Lessons Learned Centre (JALLC) in Portugal, which collects, evaluates and disseminates experiences from experimentation and operations, and the Joint Forces Training Centre in Bydgoszcz in Poland

[905] The European Union

[906] In parallel with the sweeping changes in NATO, European cooperation in the field of security and defense policy is also undergoing significant development

[907] The EU has recently strengthened its ambition to pursue a common foreign and security policy

[908] Common Foreign and Security Policy – CFSP) by adopting a security policy strategy (the Solana paper) that advocates a more forceful and united foreign policy

[909] This ambition is also demonstrated by the fact that the EU's European Security and Defence Policy (ESDP) has been strengthened in recent years, both at the political and practical level

[910] The proposal for a new constitutional treaty was not adopted in December 2003, but defense policy cooperation emerged from the meeting strengthened

[911] This will have significant consequences for the EU's defence policy dimension through the development of closer and more integrated cooperation in defence-related research, the development of capabilities and equipment procurement, as well as the establishment of structures that will strengthen the Union's operational capability

[912] In sum, the EU wants to become a more visible and coordinated foreign policy actor, and will in the future play an increasing role in European security and stability

[913] The deepening of security and defence policy cooperation in the EU is taking place partly through arrangements agreed between NATO and the EU, where NATO can, within established procedures, provide collective military resources and capabilities to EU-led operations

[914] However, the EU also relies on being able to carry out so-called autonomous operations, based solely on its own resources, as identified through the EU's own force register

[915] Through concrete operations, the EU has demonstrated its ability to play an independent operational role

[916] The operations in Congo (ARTEMIS), in Bosnia (EUPM) and in Macedonia (PROXIMA) are concrete examples in this regard

[917] At the same time, the EU has demonstrated its ability to cooperate with other international organizations such as NATO and the UN, and to include non-EU countries in its operational activities

[918] However, challenges remain both for the EU's own defence and security policy, and for the EU's relations with NATO and allies that are not members of the EU

[919] The previous political disagreement within the EU on the development of the ESDP has been largely resolved through the agreement reached in December

[920] Nevertheless, there is still some way to go until the EU has a common defense policy

[921] The EU still lacks important military capabilities that are necessary to be able to carry out larger and demanding military operations, not least if these are to be carried out at short notice and in more remote areas

[922] The defense budgets of EU countries are under considerable pressure, and the ability 2003–2004 St.prp

[923] The further modernization of the Armed Forces in the period 2005–2008 and the willingness to prioritize new military capabilities, as well as to carry out the necessary rationalization and restructuring, are variable

[924] The EU's ability to conduct independent military operations has nevertheless gradually come into place, and developments within the EU towards giving greater weight to the defence dimension could accelerate this process further

[925] The security policy division of roles between NATO and the EU has still not been finally clarified

[926] The risk of duplication and competition with NATO is present in this regard, all depending on which specific solutions are developed in the future

[927] For Norway, the concrete practice of the participation rights for allied non-EU countries in connection with EU-led operations is very important

[928] As a participant and non-EU country, Norway can take part in the day-to-day management of an operation

[929] However, Norway has limited influence over the political management of EU operations

[930] Norway's ability to influence the development of ESDP is minimal

[931] It is of fundamental importance to Norway that cooperation between the EU and NATO remains constructive and is based on openness, cooperation and mutual coordination

[932] It is also important that the two organizations do not develop competing structures

[933] Perhaps Norway's most important contribution in this regard will be to follow up on the Allied intentions that are being realized through the work on the NRF, the new command structure and the PCC, so that NATO becomes an effective security policy instrument seen from both sides of the Atlantic

[934] Furthermore, the close cooperation within the framework of the North Sea Strategy will also contribute to linking us more strongly to countries that are central to the development of the EU's security and defence policy

[935] An active Norwegian European policy, which seeks real Norwegian influence in the EU's military crisis management, is crucial to safeguarding Norwegian interests in a changing Europe

[936] This is also a prerequisite for Norway to be able to contribute to a strengthened European crisis management capacity

[937] The United States and the transatlantic dimension

[938] It is only recently that the structural consequences of the end of the Cold War are truly beginning to become apparent

[939] The United States' dominant position in international politics, and the fact that national security has gained increased importance in American politics, have significant implications for US policy in the international arena and towards Europe

[940] The changing risk landscape has led to new patterns of international cooperation, which is evident above all through the fight against terrorism

[941] Early re enemies collaborate to counter, limit and, if necessary, combat new and common threats

[942] The undramatic termination of the ABM (Anti-Ballistic Missile) Treaty in June 2002 and the Russian-American agreement of May 2002, which limits active strategic nuclear warheads to between 1,700 and 2,200, are expressions of important changes in the strategic situation

[943] The above-mentioned agreement between the United States and Russia also opens up cooperation on defense against ballistic missiles

[944] This topic is discussed, among other things, within the framework of the NATO-Russia Council (NRC) within NATO

[945] Another feature of the new strategic picture is greater political differences between the United States and some key European allies, which in selected areas has led to more marked conflicts of interest

[946] Such contradictions have been partly exacerbated by the fact that the security policy division of roles between the EU and NATO, and with it also between the EU and the US, is still in the making

[947] On the American side, it seems that the ambitions of some European allies to increase the EU's role as a security and defense policy actor in areas that have traditionally been NATO's domain are unfortunate

[948] At the same time, the American experiences from Iraq and Afghanistan have demonstrated the importance of having European allies as active contributors

[949] Transatlantic ties are still strong, and the above-mentioned contradictions should therefore not be exaggerated

[950] The old shared destiny from the Cold War has changed, but not gone

[951] The mutual dependence was obvious in the face of the threat from the Soviet Union

[952] With the disappearance of this threat, mutual dependence is naturally less prominent, but the Euro-Atlantic ties are built on fundamental mutual dependence and common values, which go beyond politics and economics

[953] At the same time, one should not underestimate the difficulties that arise from institutional conditions, different threat perceptions, imbalances in military strength across the Atlantic, and different approaches to handling new security challenges

[954] This creates challenges, also for Norway

[1151] Holistic approach to the use of security policy instruments During the Cold War, military power played an absolutely dominant role in meeting the real existential threat that the Soviet Union represented

[1154] The Armed Forces will continue to constitute a key security policy instrument

[1156] In some cases, especially in the early stages of a disaster or crisis, or when situations or armed conflicts are so dangerous that others cannot operate in them, military forces will often be the only security policy instrument available that can be used effectively and with the necessary degree of safety for personnel

[1157] There is a great risk that conflicts, crises and emergencies involving the use of armed force will arise in the future

[1158] In the initial phases, military forces may also have to contribute to solving tasks that normally require other security positions
