[1166] The framework for Norwegian use of military power

[1167] When it comes to the use of military force, it may initially be useful to distinguish between legality and legitimacy

[1168] The use of military force is legal when it has a basis in international law

[1169] It is legitimate when it can be justified politically and morally

[1170] In international politics

[1171] However, it can often be difficult to clearly distinguish between politics, law and morality

[1172] The need for legality and political legitimacy – both domestically and internationally – will be crucial for Norway's use of military force

[1173] The use of military force must be anchored in international law, either through the consent of the parties (e.g. a peacekeeping operation where the warring parties seek military intervention from a third party to achieve a ceasefire), through the right of self-defense under Article 51 of the UN Charter, or through a mandate from the UN Security Council under Chapter VI or VII of the UN Charter

[1174] The right to self-defense also includes the right to support a state that is attacked militarily, without a specific mandate from the UN Security Council

[1175] There is broad agreement in Norway that Norwegian participation in military operations outside Norway must have a solid foundation in international law

[1176] Should it prove impossible to obtain express authorization for the use of force from the UN Security Council (cf. the veto power of the permanent members) in a situation that poses a threat to international peace and security, an assessment must be made, if necessary, of whether there may still be a basis under international law for the active use of military means

[1177] In such an assessment, political and moral legitimacy will weigh heavily

[1178] Only in exceptional cases should Norwegian forces participate in operations that do not have a mandate from the UN, and then only when this is well-founded based on international law considerations

[1179] For Norway, it is primarily only appropriate to use military means of force on a purely national basis in certain and limited situations, primarily related to asserting sovereignty, exercising authority and managing crises and incidents

[1180] In all other situations, the Armed Forces will participate within a multinational framework – in or outside Norway

[1181] Central Norwegian security interests, the international framework, considerations of international peace and security, alliance solidarity and humanitarian considerations will, to a particular extent, determine the extent to which and how Norwegian authorities will use the Armed Forces as a security policy instrument

[1182] Norway has limited military resources, and will not participate in all types of military operations or under all conditions

[1183] International solidarity, and especially alliance solidarity, will nevertheless provide strong guidance that indicates Norwegian participation in the operations that we support

[1227] If developments make it reasonable to conclude that we are facing a changed global development direction in the medium and longer term, with perhaps more serious security challenges than originally assumed, it is important to be able to adjust the direction of the Armed Forces in accordance with this

[1228] The defense will consequently need a high level of flexibility, availability and adaptability, both to meet a wide range of possible security challenges in the near future, and possibly more extensive changes in global developments in the longer term

[1229] This requires the ability and willingness to undergo military transformation, with the aim of being at the forefront of developments to the greatest extent possible and avoiding becoming stuck in established patterns of thought

[1230] The ongoing restructuring of the Armed Forces, and credible Norwegian participation in the further development of NATO, constitute key prerequisites for achieving this

[1231] Norwegian security can only be safeguarded in partnership with others

[1232] Through multinational initiatives such as the North Sea Strategy, PCC and NRF, and through participation in specific operations together with our allies and other partners, we contribute to shaping our security policy framework and the Armed Forces in a direction that benefits our own security and strengthens our ability to handle new security challenges, in Norway and in Norwegian areas as well as in a broader international perspective

[1233] The further modernization of the Armed Forces in the period 2005–

[1234] Technological and material framework conditions for defense policy and the design of the Armed Forces

[1235] In addition to the developments that characterize Norway's security policy environment and that are discussed above, several other factors are also of great importance to the Armed Forces

[1236] This applies above all to technological development and developments within international material cooperation

[1237] These are described below

[1238] Technological developments, network-based defense and technological cost-cutting

[1239] Technological developments are of crucial importance for how military forces are assembled and for how military operations are led and conducted

[1240] The use of modern technology creates both new threats and vulnerabilities, and new opportunities to solve military tasks in more effective ways

[1241] The spread of advanced technology and modern society's critical dependence on technology to function have created fertile ground for new security challenges

[1242] The danger of the spread of weapons of mass destruction and modern weapons technology is central to this picture

[1243] Technological developments have also created new opportunities to target both civilian society and military opponents using new instruments and asymmetric strategies

[1244] The consequences of lagging behind in technological development could in some cases be of decisive negative significance, both for the ability to strike an adversary in an effective and differentiated manner, and for the ability to effectively protect one's own military forces and population

[1245] At the same time, technological developments have created new opportunities and greater flexibility in working to meet security challenges

[1246] The development of new precision-guided weapons, surveillance systems and new information and communication systems are examples of this

[1247] This has, among other things, contributed to creating weapons systems and units that individually, and compared to previously, have a greater effect, are less personnel-intensive and in many cases reduce the chance of own losses

[1248] The latter does not mean that technology can always support personnel

[1249] A number of military operations will also have to be personnel-intensive in the future

[1250] Technological development does not in itself reduce the requirement for protection of one's own forces, but can be used as one of several means to make protection more effective

[1251] Today, it is primarily developments in information technology that are helping to change weapons, equipment and the way modern military organizations operate

[1252] In the longer term, developments in information technology will probably have even greater consequences for the development of the Norwegian defense

[1253] To date, technological innovations have mainly been exploited to improve existing ways of operating

[1254] However, technological advances can only be fully exploited when established operating patterns are fundamentally changed

[1255] This will be central to the development of the Armed Forces in the period 2005–

[1256] The development towards a network-based response (NBF) is a result of the new possibilities offered by information technology

[1257] This is a concept that focuses on how military operations can be conducted more effectively, by linking units, across the branches of defense and at different levels of the organization, in a network using information technology

[1258] This is described in more detail in box

[1259] Technological developments also have important consequences for cost developments

[1260] The rise in prices for military materiel and equipment is creating both pressure on the Armed Forces' finances and uncertainty in defense planning

[1261] The development of technology is increasingly led by civilian, commercial actors

[1262] This basically means that modern technology is often more easily accessible and more affordable than before

[1263] Nevertheless, in many cases, adapting and applying technology for military purposes proves to be costly

[1264] At the same time, the unit costs of modern defense equipment tend to increase significantly from one generation to the next

[1265] This is a development over which we have very little influence, because it is largely driven by the demand of the major nations

[1266] Technological cost-cutting is thus a key element in the long-term

[1267] No. 42 2003–

[1268] The further modernization of the Armed Forces in the period 2005–2008 will shape defense planning

[1269] The pace and extent of this type of cost growth is difficult to predict accurately, especially in the longer term

[1270] This will depend, among other things, on the effects of technological innovations, their pace, the extent of multinational cooperation, which capabilities are specifically acquired, whether we choose standardized ("off-the-shelf") or specialized solutions, and on our ability to integrate these in a cost effective manner into the defense structure

[1271] The risk picture and technological developments are therefore pointing in the same direction with regard to the specific design of the Armed Forces

[1272] A relevant defense must have a technological standard that makes it possible to operate effectively, alone and together with allied forces, inside and outside Norway and across the entire spectrum of conflicts

[1273] To achieve this, we must take into account the pace of modernization of our allies and the potential challenges we may face, and exploit the opportunities inherent in technological development

[1274] With its limited resources, it must

[1275] Norway will mainly acquire fully developed equipment, or alternatively develop modern technology and capacities through collaboration with others

[1276] Trends in international materiel cooperation

[1277] The defense market is one of the least open and free markets in the international economy

[1278] While there is a stated desire for open and international competition to ensure fair procurement and better utilization of research and development funds, many nations consider the ability to deliver defense equipment as an integral part of their defense capability, and thus as a central aspect of defense and security policy

[1279] Furthermore, there are strong national industrial policy interests linked to the defense market

[1280] Protectionism and export restrictions are still prominent features in this picture

[1281] In particular, the United States has introduced strict restrictions on the export of a number of types of defense technology

[1282] A main challenge in this connection lies in the tension between the desire for national control and a growing need for international cooperation

[1283] This creates significant challenges in the processes surrounding the acquisition of new defense equipment, which is also evident in the relatively slow progress in the work to achieve more effective cooperation between the procurement activities of different nations

[1284] Despite the challenges associated with creating good international cooperation arrangements in this area, multinational cooperation related to the acquisition and development of defense equipment has become increasingly important for smaller countries and their defense industries

[1285] The complexity and costs associated with the development of modern defense equipment make it more demanding for small nations with limited resources to develop and maintain modern military capabilities on their own, and it also makes it more difficult to operate in an integrated manner with other countries

[1286] At the same time, this also makes it increasingly difficult for smaller companies to capture market share on their own

[1287] The development of the defense industry is characterized by consolidation, restructuring and alliance building

[1288] This is especially true within the defense industry in Europe, where the development over several years has been towards fewer but larger players, not least in order to meet the competition from the industrial giants in the United States

[1289] This is reinforced by the general economic challenges many European countries face in their defense policy

[1290] In such a situation, there are increased demands for streamlining material procurement

[1291] This trend also fulfills an overarching political function, by supporting the EU's development of an independent European security and defense policy

[1292] Norway has a strategic interest in contributing to the development of new defence equipment within both a European and a broader international framework

[1293] This is not least in consideration of the operational needs of the Armed Forces, including the ability to operate effectively with allies and to be able to develop and maintain the necessary expertise, but also based on the requirement for cost-effectiveness, in order to be able to influence developments in international materiel cooperation and in consideration of our own defense industry

[1294] Norway therefore participates in international material cooperation, both within a bilateral and a multilateral framework

[1295] For Norway, it is important that there are real industrial policy alternatives in both the US and Europe, and that we can freely choose between the alternatives

[1296] In NATO, Norway participates in the Conference of National Armaments Directors (CNAD

[1297] This group sets the framework for cooperation on large material projects within the alliance framework, but rarely has decisive influence over the specific development of individual projects or on the choice of suppliers

[1298] Norway also participates in WEAG (Western European Armaments Group) and in Nordic Armaments Cooperation (NORDAC

[1299] In addition, Norway has entered into agreements and established material projects with selected partner countries

[1300] This applies primarily to the countries that are part of the North Sea Strategy (cf. box 3.4), but also to other important partners, above all the USA

[1301] From the Norwegian side, the developments with regard to WEAG are particularly worrying

[1302] The EU has taken the initiative to establish a new cooperation body for the development and acquisition of defence equipment, which will have many of the functions currently under WEAG, particularly in areas such as the harmonisation of equipment acquisitions, as well as research and development (cf. box

[1303] As a result, WEAG is expected to close down

[1304] This means that Norway will lose the influence we have had there, and there is great uncertainty about what role and influence a Norway outside the EU will be able to achieve in the new cooperation body (which currently has the working title Agency in the field of Defence Capabilities Development, Research, Acquisition and Armament

[1305] The creation of this new organization thus represents a significant challenge for Norway

[1306] From the Norwegian side, it is serious that we could end up in a situation where, at a strategic level, we do not have access to any material cooperation organizations in Europe

[1307] Such participation is important not only to underpin our desire for closer defense and operational cooperation with our closest European allies, but also to give Norway insight into, and opportunities to influence, broader political structures and processes that we would otherwise not have

[1308] It is therefore important to follow developments closely with a view to achieving good collaborative relations as early as possible with the new organization

[1309] At the same time, great emphasis must be placed on identifying new areas where bilateral or multilateral solutions can be developed for the development, purchase and operation of Box 4.1 EU defence equipment cooperation The EU is working to establish a cooperation body for the development and acquisition of defence equipment

[1310] Currently, this body has the working title Agency in the Field of Defence Capabilities Development, Research, Acquisition and Armament

[1311] In the autumn of 2003, the work was led by the Italian EU Presidency through an ad hoc planning group

[1312] The work will be continued during the Irish Presidency in the spring

[1313] The plan is to have a new Agency established by the end of

[1315] This is expected to conclude its work during the spring of 2004. material with selected strategic partners

[1316] Here too, the North Sea Strategy will be able to help counteract some of the disadvantages of standing outside the EU and its underlying organizations

[1317] In many cases, close cooperation with a smaller group of like-minded countries will be able to yield greater results than institutionalized cooperation within the framework of larger formal cooperation forums, which are often characterized by a number of different and conflicting interests

[1318] The security policy developments described in Chapter 3 and the conditions described in this chapter together form the overall framework for the Armed Forces' orientation, tasks and capabilities

[1321] The further modernization of the Armed Forces in the period 2005–2008 The Armed Forces' orientation, tasks and capabilities

[1322] The defense must be organized and further developed within the framework of a holistic approach

[1323] The sum of the most central strategic developments and challenges that characterize the framework conditions for the response must be taken into account, as described in the previous chapters

[1324] These all point in the same direction, and require a modern, flexible and alliance-adapted defense that can be deployed where and when the need arises, whether the tasks are to be solved at home or abroad, alone or together with others

[1325] This defense can only be created and maintained through extensive multinational cooperation, mainly with allies and within the NATO framework

[1326] Only through close cooperation with our allies can we maintain a modern and flexible defense, in terms of technology, organization, use of resources and expertise

[1327] This means that Norway, in order to achieve even better defense, should actively follow up on the transformation process that has been initiated in NATO

[1328] This is of paramount importance for the Armed Forces' ability to carry out its tasks effectively, not least for the Armed Forces' ability to handle episodes and crises in Norwegian areas alone and at short notice

[1329] The Armed Forces must be organized in such a way that the greatest possible correspondence is created between what the Armed Forces are expected to be able to do and what the Armed Forces can do in practice

[1330] This consistency must be sought through the formulation of the main elements of defence policy – the defence policy objectives, the tasks of the Defence Force and the defence concept

[1331] The defence policy thus links the overall political ambitions for the role and function of the Armed Forces as a central instrument in Norwegian security policy, with the specific design of the structure, organisation and activities of the Armed Forces

[1332] Main elements of defense policy Through the consideration of Recommendation

[1338] The Government believes that the basic content of defense policy should remain unchanged

[1339] There is still a need for adjustments, clarifications and simplifications in line with developments within and outside the Armed Forces, so that a comprehensive and logical connection is established between security policy, defence policy and developments in the structure and organisation of the Armed Forces

[1340] Defence policy goals

[1341] The armed forces must be organised so that they appear as a relevant and effective instrument in the work of achieving the overarching security policy goals (cf. Chapter

[1342] This must be reflected in the overall objectives for the Armed Forces' activities

[1343] The defence policy objectives shall constitute a link between defence policy and security policy, by specifying what the Armed Forces shall contribute to ensure the greatest possible achievement of the overall security policy objectives

[1344] It is the government's view that the existing defense policy goals do not fulfill this function in an appropriate manner

[1345] The existing goals are not very suitable as a management tool for the Armed Forces' activities at a higher level

[1346] With their primary focus on capability and capacities, these overlap significantly with the discussion of the Armed Forces' operational capability, which naturally

[1347] should be linked to the formulation and content of the tasks, and to the subsequent description of the operational structure

[1348] The government is therefore proposing new defense policy goals, which are more directly derived from the overarching security policy goals, and which thus create a better connection between security and defense policy

[1349] In the government's view, the defense policy goals for the next long-term period should be that the Armed Forces, within its area of responsibility and through cooperation with other national authorities where this is natural, should be able to

[1350] No. 42 The further modernization of the Armed Forces in the period 2005–2008 – Alone and together with allies, secure Norwegian sovereignty, Norwegian rights and interests, and preserve Norwegian freedom of action against military and other pressure; – together with allies, through participation in several national peace operations and international defense cooperation, contribute to peace, stability, enforcement of international law and respect for human rights, and prevent the use of force by states and non-state actors against Norway and NATO; – together with allies, contribute to the collective defense of Norway and other allies in accordance with our alliance commitments, and to meet various types of attacks and attacks with coercive force to ensure Norwegian and collective security; – contribute to safeguarding Norwegian societal security, saving lives and limiting the consequences of accidents, disasters, attacks and attacks from state and non-state actors

[1351] In summary, the changed defense policy goals imply a greater focus on what the Armed Forces should achieve, rather than how this should be achieved

[1352] The following description of the Armed Forces' tasks and the basic principles of the defence concept constitute an operationalization of the above-mentioned defence policy objectives, and of how the Armed Forces should be organised to achieve them

[1353] In extension of this, the tasks form the basis for the specific design of the Armed Forces' capabilities and structure

[1354] The tasks of the Armed Forces

[1355] The absence of a single, defining threat means that the Armed Forces will have to fulfil several different roles in the future, both at home and abroad, cf. chapter 3.8.3. In order to fulfil these roles, the Armed Forces must be able to solve their specific tasks in an effective manner

[1356] Through the performance of its tasks, the Armed Forces shall contribute to fulfilling Norway's security and defense policy goals

[1357] The Armed Forces' tasks thus also form the basis for the design of the Armed Forces' activities, expertise, capacities and operational capabilities

[1358] The operational capability of the Armed Forces concerns the ability of the Armed Forces to carry out its assigned tasks, and is subject to an annual evaluation

[1359] Strengthening the operational capability of the Norwegian Armed Forces is the main objective of the ongoing modernization of the Armed Forces

[1360] The Government assumes that there is no need for extensive changes in the actual content of the Armed Forces' existing tasks

[1361] However, there is a need to establish a clearer connection between the Armed Forces' tasks and the overall security and defense policy goals, as well as to create a more logical presentation of the tasks that simultaneously implies a clearer delineation and specification of the level of ambition

[1362] This will help make the tasks better suited as a management tool for the Armed Forces' activities

[1363] The tasks of the Armed Forces are divided into "national tasks", "tasks that are solved in cooperation with allies and possibly others" and "other tasks

[1364] The first two categories should – as a balanced whole – guide the structural development of the Armed Forces

[1365] This means that the national and international tasks are not in conflict or competition, but on the contrary, should complement each other so that mutually reinforcing synergies are created between the different aspects of the Armed Forces' activities

[1366] The Armed Forces' capabilities should primarily be able to be used both at home and abroad, and in principle there will be no distinction between personnel/ capabilities for national and international missions, respectively

[1367] Other tasks" should not in themselves be of significance for strengthening the structure, but should be solved to the extent possible with the structure established to handle the first two categories of tasks

[1368] However, the third category of tasks is also of such a nature that in certain, clearly defined areas it may require the development and maintenance of a special operational capability

[1369] National tasks

[1370] A number of the Armed Forces' tasks arise from a Norwegian responsibility in Norway and nearby Norwegian areas

[1371] They must therefore be resolved nationally, and initially without allied involvement

[1372] These tasks require a permanently high availability of, and presence of, operational military capabilities under Norwegian control

[1373] The national tasks of the Armed Forces will be: – to ensure a national basis for decision-making through timely surveillance and intelligence

[1374] The Armed Forces shall be responsible for effective information gathering and monitoring of Norwegian areas of interest

[1375] This includes an intelligence and security service that, in close collaboration with the political and military leadership, and through contact with international partners, continuously collects, processes and analyses information about various state and non-state actors, capacities, phenomena and trends

[1376] A good situational picture must be maintained with the aim of continuously further developing a satisfactory basis for decision-making, including notification, so that the Armed Forces can carry out the St.prop

[1377] No. 42 2003–

[1378] The further modernization of the Armed Forces in the period 2005–2008 its other tasks effectively, and Norwegian authorities can be kept continuously informed. – to enforce Norwegian sovereignty

[1379] The Armed Forces shall contribute to ensuring Norwegian sovereignty and preserving national integrity

[1380] This includes deterrence and handling of limited episodes, as well as preventing unauthorized actors from accessing Norwegian territory and from harming vital societal interests

[1381] Assertion of sovereignty requires the ability to handle incidents on land, in territorial waters and in Norwegian airspace

[1382] The task also includes, if necessary, securing Norwegian embassies and Norwegian shipping

[1383] Effective and credible assertion of sovereignty requires that the Armed Forces have sufficient resources to both monitor activity in Norwegian areas and to be able to be present at short notice with suitable units. – to safeguard Norwegian exercise of authority in demarcated areas The Armed Forces shall safeguard the exercise of authority related to the protection of Norwegian sovereign rights and the enforcement of Norwegian law in those areas where the Armed Forces has been granted such authority

[1384] This also includes preventive measures

[1385] The exercise of the Armed Forces' authority is linked to supervisory and control activities on behalf of other public agencies, and is exercised in peacetime primarily by the border guard forces and the Coast Guard

[1386] The exercise of authority is a task that should be of dimension to the Armed Forces in the sense that it requires an operational capability that is also relevant to the Armed Forces' other tasks, primarily the assertion of sovereignty, and thus creates important synergy effects within the Armed Forces

[1387] Furthermore, the task must be solved in a way that does not create significant operational or financial limitations for the Defence Forces' other activities. – to prevent and handle incidents and security policy crises in Norway and Norwegian areas The Defence Forces shall contribute to handling national security policy incidents and crises that are led in their entirety by Norwegian political authorities, and which are not of such a scale that the government would want to involve the alliance

[1388] Such episodes and crises – including terrorist attacks – must be brought under control quickly, and with a minimum of negative consequences, on Norwegian terms

[1389] The task also includes the ability to quickly ensure that a situation is handled so that it is covered by Article 5 of the Atlantic Pact, if Norwegian authorities wish for the alliance to be involved, or are unable to handle it alone

[1390] It will be important to avoid situations where crises that are too big for Norway are too small for NATO

[1391] Without an independent ability to handle crises of varying scope and nature, Norway could lose credibility, both in relation to potential counterparts and in the NATO context

[1392] Effective management and coordination, both internally within the Armed Forces and between the Armed Forces and civilian actors, will constitute important prerequisites for solving this task

[1393] Furthermore, available and flexible military forces, with short reaction times, are required within all branches of defense and in the Home Guard

[1394] Tasks that are solved in cooperation with allies and possibly others

[1395] The most demanding tasks related to the defense of Norway and NATO, as well as tasks related to international stabilization and peace-building work, must be solved by the Armed Forces in collaboration with others

[1396] Here, Norway will only provide a limited share of the military capabilities needed

[1397] These tasks will be: – to contribute to the collective defense of Norway and other parts of NATO against threats, attacks and attacks, including the use of weapons of mass destruction. The Armed Forces shall, together with our allies, meet threats, attacks and attacks on Norway and other parts of NATO that are covered by Articles 5 and 6 of the Atlantic Treaty

[1398] This includes conventional attacks, attacks with weapons of mass destruction, as well as other types of attacks and threats – from both state and non-state actors – that cause or threaten to cause such extensive damage that it is appropriate for NATO to implement collective countermeasures

[1399] A key element of this task is to help NATO as a whole ensure a credible deterrent capability, so that risks and threats do not arise, and to contribute to the Alliance's overall ability to deal with new unconventional threats, attacks and attacks that are covered by the collective defence obligation

[1400] In the future, this task could also include the protection of geographical areas and the civilian population against potential missile attacks

[1401] At the same time, there may be a need to safeguard Norwegian and allied security through participation in operations outside the alliance's traditional core area

[1402] – to contribute to multinational crisis management, including multinational peace operations 2003–2004 St.prop

[1404] The procedures for assistance to the police are regulated in the instructions for the Armed Forces' assistance to the police, established by Royal Decree of 28 February

[1405] The main points of the instructions are

[1406] – The instructions assume that the police request assistance

[1407] It is further assumed that the Norwegian Defence can assist when it is compatible with the Norwegian Defence's primary tasks, and the police's own personnel and/or material resources are not sufficient

[1408] – The police's tasks are in principle the same in peace, crisis and war

[1409] There may be a need for assistance from the Armed Forces also in crisis and war

[1410] The instruction is therefore no longer limited to applying "in peace

[1411] – The number of types of assistance is grouped into three: 1) administrative assistance, which includes assistance with transport or other administrative support that does not involve the Armed Forces in the police operational task solution; 2) operational assistance, which includes assistance in connection with accidents, natural disasters, the neutralization and removal of explosives, etc.; and 3) enforcement assistance, which includes assistance in searching for and apprehending dangerous persons, as well as in the event of a threat of widespread or other attacks

[1412] particularly harmful in nature directed against essential societal interests

[1413] – The role of the Norwegian Police Directorate in connection with requests and decisions about assistance from the Norwegian Defence Forces is regulated

[1414] – The need for close cooperation between the police and the Armed Forces through training and development of coordinated plans, procedures and regular joint exercises is emphasized more strongly than in the previous instructions

[1415] The assistance categories and framework assumptions in the current instructions on the Armed Forces' assistance to the police, combined with the police's intelligence information and assessment of their own competence, personnel and material resources, will form the basis for assessing which situations should be handled through the Armed Forces providing assistance to the police

[1416] In addition to operational assistance in connection with the decontamination or removal of explosives, etc., there is, however, reason to mention the following situations where assistance may be relevant

[1417] – Use of the Armed Forces' helicopters in connection with the search and arrest of dangerous persons, as well as assistance during state visits

[1418] – Hostage, terrorist and sabotage situations onshore and offshore, where, given the circumstances, there is no basis for claiming that a security policy situation exists or that the situation is otherwise assumed to have a security policy dimension

[1419] The instructions for the Armed Forces' assistance to the police are based on the fact that the additional costs incurred by the Armed Forces shall be covered by the requesting authority, unless otherwise stipulated or agreed

[1420] The Armed Forces shall, within the framework of international law, be able to contribute military capabilities with the aim of creating control over various situations that either threaten common security and vital interests, or that have other unacceptable consequences

[1421] Such crisis management could encompass all types of security policy challenges, in principle could take place all over the world, be led by established organizations such as the UN, NATO and the EU, or be implemented as part of timelimited coalitions

[1422] For this to be possible, personnel in all branches of defense must be available for both national and international missions

[1423] The task includes preventive and stabilizing operations, where the purpose is to prevent an acute crisis from arising through the preventive deployment of forces, for example to prevent the outbreak of an armed conflict or the occurrence of serious violations of international law, including widespread violations of human rights

[1424] Furthermore, the task includes the utilization of military capacities to maintain control and contribute to positive development in the longer term

[1425] Other tasks

[1426] These are tasks for which other authorities have primary responsibility

[1427] These tasks should not be limiting for the Armed Forces' orientation, and must therefore be primarily solved with the capacities and expertise that are available, based on the ability to solve the tasks described above

[1441] The Defence Concept The Defence Concept defines how the Defence Forces should be organised to best be able to carry out the tasks assigned to them, and thereby contribute to realising the overall security and defence policy goals

[1442] The defense concept shall describe the basic idea of the organization of the Armed Forces, and thus indicate the overall direction in this regard

[1443] As a vision for the development of the Armed Forces, the defense concept should have an explanatory, guiding and focusing effect

[1444] The Government will therefore formulate the defence concept in a more normative direction, which provides a concise and comprehensive description of the most central principles that will form the basis for the future development and activities of the Armed Forces

[1445] The Defence Forces shall be developed as a modern, flexible and alliance-adapted security policy instrument, striving for a balance between the Defence Forces' tasks, structure and access to resources

[1446] The activities shall be based on close cooperation with relevant civil authorities and on a duty of protection that is practiced in line with the needs of the Armed Forces

[1447] The focus should be on securing and promoting Norwegian interests, through being able to handle a broad spectrum of challenges both nationally and internationally

[1448] This means that the central principles underlying the existing defense concept will be continued

[1449] At the same time, a necessary adaptation and further development of these is reflected, in light of developments within and outside the Armed Forces

[1450] The new Defence must reflect the changing security policy picture and the uncertainty that will continue to surround it (be modern and flexible), and be adapted to the requirements and opportunities that cooperation within NATO and with allies entails (be alliance-friendly

[1451] Furthermore, it must reflect the need for strengthened and changed civil-military cooperation and a continuation of conscription (be socially integrated), and be geared towards the specific tasks that are actually to be solved at home and abroad (be task-based

[1462] The basic principle of the total defense concept has been that society's total resources, if necessary also private resources, should be able to be deployed to support the defense of Norway, to handle acute and precarious security challenges in war or when war threatens

[1463] The total defence concept has been based on special authorisation laws (emergency legislation) and the Armed Forces' need for support when the conditions for using these authorisations have been met

[1464] The concept has therefore not included the lower crisis levels

[1465] Comprehensive and mandatory civilian support to the Armed Forces in serious crisis situations will still require that emergency preparedness legislation can be applied

[1466] Civilian support to the Armed Forces in situations where emergency legislation does not apply is based on commercial arrangements, as well as on cooperation with and support from civilian authorities

[1467] Such schemes will also be relevant for civilian support that cannot be provided even if it is permitted under emergency legislation

[1468] This could, for example, be inventories that no longer exist, or resources that experience has shown become scarce in crisis situations

[1469] Civil security and emergency preparedness work in general, and specifically aimed at critical infrastructure and business, can also be seen as civilian support, as robustness in these systems helps the Armed Forces function in a situation where it increasingly relies on purely civilian systems and deliveries

[1470] The changing threat and risk landscape, particularly the rise of international terrorism, has led to an increased importance of societal security

[1471] It is necessary to see the traditional total defense approach in light of this development

[1472] Central to today's civil security work is the protection of the civilian population and vital societal interests in situations where there is no traditional military threat

[1473] Reference is also made to the visions and objectives for social security work that were laid down in Recommendation

[1474] No. 9 (2002–

[1475] Questions may be raised about the extent to which it is appropriate to use the concept of total defence regarding society's preparedness against threats and risks other than military challenges affecting Norwegian territory

[1477] The concept of total defence is also used in the regulations, where a change to the concept may necessitate changes to the regulations

[1478] On the other hand, it may also be desirable, through the use of terminology, to emphasize that state authorities take the new security challenges very seriously

[1479] Total defense is a well-established concept with wide support

[1480] It is desirable to benefit from and build on the expertise and commitment that has been developed over half a century within total defence to meet a broader range of challenges

[1523] The preparedness and force building system

[1524] The preparedness system for the Armed Forces and the Civilian Preparedness System aims to achieve a coordinated implementation of preparedness actions to prevent or reduce the extent of damage, as well as to strengthen national preparedness in crisis situations

[1525] The system contains measures that describe pre-planned actions as well as procedures for information exchange that the Norwegian Defence and civil authorities can quickly implement

[1526] The overall preparedness system is under review with the aim of adapting it better to security policy challenges in the lower end of the crisis spectrum, including asymmetric threats such as terrorism, attacks with weapons of mass destruction and attacks against information systems

[1527] The protection of critical infrastructure and civilians is given a greater role than in the current system

[1528] The system can also be used as a supplement to other planning for crises of a non-security nature, such as natural disasters

[1529] The goal is to complete the audit of the emergency preparedness system during

[1530] The structure of the revised preparedness system will be adapted to NATO's

[1531] crisis management system (NATO Crisis Response System – NCRS) to provide increased ability to cooperate with our allies and other nations in the event of a crisis

[1532] At the same time, the system must meet national needs, including the total defense concept and the mobilization system

[1533] The system contains a number of measures within various subject areas

[1534] This makes it possible to implement measures adapted to the individual situation

[1535] The measures vary in scope, from those that have few social consequences to more extensive measures that require the application of emergency legislation

[1536] The national emergency preparedness system will be able to be used together with allies and other nations, alone and when handling crises both in Norway and outside Norway

[1537] Through the proposals put forward in this bill, the proportion of standing and available forces in the Armed Forces will increase in relation to the proportion of mobilization forces

[1538] Although the size of the mobilization force is reduced, mobilization units will still constitute an important part of the Armed Forces' operational structure

[1539] There will therefore also be a need in the future for a system that ensures the strength building of the mobilization units

[1540] Today's mobilization system was established to ensure the best possible utilization of the Armed Forces' resources in times of crisis, armed conflict and war

[1541] To date, the system has primarily taken care of building up the strength of the entire war organization with a view to a state of war

[1542] In the future, too, the necessary integrity in force building must be maintained

[1543] There is a need to adapt the current mobilization system to new threats, a changed defense structure and the new alignment of the Armed Forces

[1544] As a consequence of the new risk picture, all forces, both standing and mobilized, should be considered placed in the same system, but with differentiated readiness requirements

[1545] An important part of this will be further measures to enable smaller mobilization units to be activated in a simpler and more appropriate way when handling crises

[1546] The Ministry of Defence will initiate a review of the mobilization system in the course of 2004 in light of the above

[1547] The process will be carried out in close dialogue between military and affected civilian emergency response authorities

[1556] The further modernization of the Armed Forces in the period 2005–2008 The Armed Forces shall be focused on being able to handle a broad spectrum of challenges, both nationally and internationally

[1557] The Norwegian Armed Forces must be organized to be able to carry out all of its tasks in the most comprehensive, comprehensive and future-oriented manner possible, and with the built-in flexibility that international uncertainty and unpredictability require

[1558] This means that it is the force structure's overall ability to solve the sum of the prioritized tasks that should determine its composition and organization, and that no single task alone should be decisive for the design of the Armed Forces

[1559] The same structure should be able to be used both nationally and internationally

[1560] However, the ratio between the proportion of forces abroad and at home must be assessed in light of the current situation at any given time, and against the need to be able to effectively handle crises and incidents that should arise in Norway and nearby Norwegian areas

[1561] The importance of transformation for the development of the Armed Forces In order for the Armed Forces to be able to effectively solve the sum of the tasks described above, it is necessary to make further adjustments to the operational structure of the Armed Forces

[1562] The need for transformation, strict prioritization, and the necessity of creating a clear connection between the tasks the Armed Forces are set to solve and the capabilities

[1563] The Armed Forces should prioritize

[1564] are key assumptions that must be taken into account in this context

[1565] Transformation means conversion or qualitative change

[1566] Military transformation involves changing the composition and characteristics or way of operating of military forces, in a broad sense

[1567] The goal of military transformation is to create a defense that is better able to handle unpredictability and a wide range of tasks

[1568] Transformation is a continuous and proactive process, in which innovative concepts, doctrines and capabilities are developed and integrated to improve and/or make the Armed Forces more efficient, including strengthening its ability to cooperate operationally nationally and internationally

[1569] For long-term defense planning and structural development, transformation means placing increased emphasis on the Armed Forces' ability for flexibility and continuous adaptation

[1570] The military must become more adaptable

[1571] Transformation must be seen in a long-term perspective

[1572] New equipment must be phased in gradually, based on available financial resources and future available technology

[1573] It takes time to change the Armed Forces' complex organization and mindset

[1574] Transformation will thus be an ongoing process, and an important topic in several long-term plans besides this one

[1575] The figure below shows the connection and interaction between four core areas of transformation

[1576] Development of doctrines is one of these

[1577] Doctrines can be defined as basic principles for the development and use of military forces in support of political objectives

[1578] They are guidelines, but require assessments when applied in specific situations

[1579] A military doctrine describes guidelines and principles for how military power should be organized and used

[1580] In a transformation perspective, doctrines must be continuously developed, updated and changed

[1581] It must be emphasized that the doctrines are future-oriented, and at the same time reflect relevant historical lessons and experiences

[1582] Furthermore, the Armed Forces' doctrines must cover the entire spectrum of tasks and contribute to interoperability

[1583] An important part of the basis for further development of doctrines will be to draw lessons from operations carried out

[1584] The way in which operations are implemented and managed must necessarily be adapted to the individual situation, to the political objectives and to the requirements of the conflict in question

[1585] It is therefore important that experiences from operations are analyzed and assessed in a holistic context

[1586] Experiences must be systematically transformed into more general lessons, where possible

[1587] Another key aspect of transformation is technological development

[1588] This will affect the organization, management forms, operational concepts and competence needs

[1589] The possibilities and limitations of technology must be reflected in the Norwegian Armed Forces' doctrines

[1590] The ability to utilize existing and new technology as effectively as possible should be a priority area for the Armed Forces

[1632] New threats and risks The fundamental premise that makes transformation a strategic process is the recognition that future threats cannot be predicted

[1633] Response planning cannot be carried out based on one specific idea of what kind of threats one will face in the future, either in the short or long term

[1634] The threat landscape we face is diffuse, unpredictable and diverse, as described in chapter

[1635] In a rapidly changing world, the ability to quickly respond to unforeseen events is essential

[1636] If, in a crisis situation, relevant military capacity is not available in time, the political relevance of military power is weakened

[1637] The organization of the armed forces cannot therefore be based on an assumption of early warning in relation to a possible threat

[1638] Therefore, flexibility and adaptability are of crucial importance

[1639] Transformation involves an approach to the development of military capabilities and structure that accepts unpredictability as a driving force, and which thus presupposes the ability to handle a wide range of possible scenarios

[1640] Multinationality will be an important aspect of transformation

[1641] Firstly, the risk picture in a globalised world is characterised by cross-border challenges

[1642] This makes multinational cooperation crucial to achieving the goal of security

[1643] Secondly, a much-needed modernization of military forces will, in a long-term perspective, require a technological level that will be too costly to achieve nationally for most countries within NATO

[1644] Multinational solutions regarding all aspects of the Armed Forces' activities are therefore required to achieve increased

[1645] Technological development accentuates the possibilities for renewal and improvement through transformation

[1646] Developments in information technology in particular will contribute to changing the organization and alignment of the Armed Forces in the future

[1647] Transformation should enable us to get the most out of changes in, for example, technology

[1648] A central part of transformation is the implementation of Network-Based Defense (NBD), which in short involves utilizing information technology to organize the Armed Forces' operational structure and units in a collaborative network

[1649] Through sharing and exchanging information across the network, our forces gain a more complete and updated decision-making basis

[1650] The response units thus have an increased opportunity to act faster, more efficiently and precisely, in relation to what the situation requires

[1651] In order to exploit this opportunity, the speed of the decision-making process must be increased, while weapons systems and sensors must have a mobility, precision and range that is commensurate with this

[1652] Increased speed and quality in the decision-making process can be achieved, among other things, by reducing the number of command levels, using modern decision support systems and facilitating an increased degree of self-organization of the forces

[1653] This will contribute to a dramatic improvement in effectiveness in relation to resource use, and strengthen the possibilities for political control in a crisis situation

[1654] Network-based organization opens up new possibilities, and at the same time puts existing

[1655] concepts, chain of command, management styles and organization under pressure

[1656] NBF will require mental, conceptual and organizational renewal, and will be financially resource-intensive

[1657] A successful introduction of NBF thus requires both significant organizational changes in the direction described above, and that efficiency gains are realized in the logistics and support structure, which can be transferred to material investments and operational activities, cf. the recommendations in chapters 7 and 8. The NBF is responsible for competence development and must ensure that the entire education system, across the branches of defense, meets the needs and requirements of transformation

[1661] Principles for prioritizing capacities and units

[1662] The overall guidance for designing the Defence Force's force structure is that the Defence Force should be able to handle a broad spectrum of possible challenges in a flexible manner

[1663] In other words, the defense must be "scenario-robust

[1664] Most capabilities are given both a national and an international role – and Norwegian capabilities are given their relevant place in NATO's force structure

[1665] The security picture and the sum of the tasks that arise from this clearly point towards an increased need for modern, deployable forces with high responsiveness and an adapted logistics apparatus

[1666] It is therefore not very appropriate to develop structural elements that are only relevant and applicable to a narrow segment of the task spectrum

[1667] Transformation in the Norwegian context will also include a continued change in focus from force production for a large mobilization defense to the production of increased operational capability, usable units and the execution of operations

[1668] The Armed Forces must be able to deliver operational capability where and when the need arises, with a set of capabilities best suited to the current situation

[1669] The transformation aspect must be given decisive importance in connection with all investments and acquisitions of new equipment

[1670] Existing material can be made even more relevant through upgrading information and communication solutions

[1671] Transformation does not necessarily mean that existing equipment must be replaced

[1672] Measures have been taken in recent years that are already preparing the ground for transformation, including the initiation of the NBF and investment in Link-16 for the fighter aircraft, the Skjold class, and the frigates which, when fully implemented, will increase the possibility of effective cooperation with units from other branches of defense

[1673] The development towards establishing an ISTAR capacity (Intelligence, surveillance, target acquisition and reconnaissance, cf. chapter 5.6.1) is also a key contribution in this context

[1674] Development of the structure must be based on the capacities necessary to solve the tasks

[1675] In this context, capacity is understood as the ability to solve a limited part of the Armed Forces' joint

[1676] There is an important distinction between capacity and capability

[1677] Capacity is primarily related to volume, while capability is related to the ability to do something (from English, "to be capable of

[1678] In NATO, capabilities are used to a greater extent

[1679] In Norwegian, capacities – defined as above – are an established concept, also in professional military terminology

[1680] For the sake of simplicity, capacities are therefore used in this sense throughout this long-term plan

[1681] A structural element is a unit or department that contributes to providing such capacity

[1682] In light of the above, the following principles have been used as a basis for the alignment of the Armed Forces' operational structure: – Flexibility, i.e. usable capacities that cover a broad segment of the task spectrum, are prioritized over capacities with a narrow scope

[1683] High priority is given to capacities with rapid reaction and movement capabilities

[1684] – Forces that are exclusively suitable for carrying out purely national tasks shall be continued only to the extent that they meet a clearly defined national need that cannot be met in any other way

[1685] – The Armed Forces' capabilities must be complementary

[1686] structure, i.e. that the individual capacities should overlap as little as possible, and complement each other to the greatest extent possible, nationally and within NATO

[1687] – New capacities that contribute to transformation should be given high priority in relation to continuing the legacy

[1688] Already acquired and adopted structural elements shall be adapted and developed so that they can contribute to the greatest extent possible to meeting specific needs that Norway has special conditions to be able to contribute to, and that are in demand in NATO

[1689] Existing capacities are made applicable and relevant through new roles and ICT solutions

[1690] – Structural development must be in line with NATO's objectives, requirements and ambitions, which Norway has helped to shape at a political level

[1691] It should be based on bilateral and multilateral forms of cooperation where this is natural

[1692] This entails a significant responsibility for ensuring that Norwegian interests are reflected in the development of NATO's military capabilities

[1693] – The structure should also have deployable forces with lower readiness, to ensure endurance, including in traditional peacekeeping operations, and thereby for the reconstruction of conflict-affected societies

[1694] – Low priority is given to non-deployable forces that are only suitable for traditional static defense

[1695] However, a qualitatively improved H V is continued as an important part of the structure

[1700] The further modernization of the Armed Forces in the period 2005–

[1701] It is the structure's overall operational capability that is crucial to its ability to solve tasks, not the defense branch-specific elements seen in isolation

[1702] Modern military operations are normally conducted from a joint perspective, and the branch-specific affiliation of different units and departments is often less relevant

[1703] In the future, the element of joint capabilities will likely increase, and the traditional division into branches of defense will have less operational significance

[1704] In relation to the existing structure, the one recommended here will provide increased operational capability, by making larger parts of the Armed Forces' structure usable and deployable for missions across the entire spectrum of the Armed Forces' tasks

[1705] To achieve this, a number of measures are required

[1706] The most important of these measures are personnel related

[1707] The Armed Forces must be ensured a stable and predictable supply of personnel to meet requirements for quality, training standards and readiness

[1708] Several of the elements in the structure therefore have a large proportion of permanently serving officers and enlisted personnel, while the remaining positions are filled by personnel with contingency contracts

[1709] The personnel area is therefore crucial for the same units to be used nationally and internationally

[1710] This requires that personnel participate in operations abroad, which are an integral part of the Armed Forces' task portfolio, on a rotational basis

[1711] The level of preparedness must be adapted to both national requirements and contribute to meeting NATO's overall needs

[1712] For Norway, it would be appropriate to have smaller elements on high alert, while larger structural elements could have somewhat lower alertness

[1713] The latter is necessary to maintain force contributions and engagement in operations over time, or to reinforce efforts when needed

[1714] The proposed structure inherently provides a comprehensive and balanced preparedness plan in which these factors are taken into account

[1715] In an acute national crisis situation, it would be entirely possible to significantly reduce the reaction time

[1716] In relation to national tasks, the structure's increased inclusion of permanent elements, which do not depend on mobilization being initiated in order for them to be used by political authorities, will significantly increase availability and responsiveness

[1717] The Norwegian Armed Forces Task Force (FIST) has so far largely consisted of dedicated units

[1718] In the future, a larger proportion of the Armed Forces' total forces will be made usable, and the task forces will consist of elements placed on operational readiness

[1719] This means that departments and units will rotate between different tasks and assignments

[1720] The FIST concept will therefore have considerably greater flexibility than before, because the structure as a whole is being turned in this direction

[1721] Management and command structure

[1722] Strategic management and command structure

[1723] The Norwegian Armed Forces' top leadership was reorganized on 1 August 2003 in accordance with a decision by the Storting

[1724] The Chief of Defence and his strategic functions were integrated into the Ministry of Defence, the Supreme Command of the Armed Forces was abolished and the Defence Staff was established

[1725] The management team will be located in temporary premises until the new building is completed, which is planned

[1726] Experience with the reorganization so far shows that it has created significant gains in important areas, and has provided increased capacity for comprehensive strategic management of the Armed Forces

[1727] In accordance with the Storting's decision in the spring of 2001, the Armed Forces have also carried out a comprehensive reorganization of the Armed Forces' operational leadership

[1728] The command structure consists of the Joint Operations Headquarters in Stavanger with two subordinate headquarters, the Regional Command Northern Norway (LDKN) in Bodø and the Regional Command Southern Norway (LDKS) in Trondheim

[1729] NATO's new Joint Warfare Center (JWC), colocated with Joint Operations Headquarters in Stavanger and under Allied Command Transformation (ACT), was established when the former Joint Headquarters North was closed in October

[1730] The tasks are new and consist of forward-looking planning, education and joint training of the operational NATO headquarters

[1731] It is considered very valuable for Norway and the Norwegian Armed Forces that a NATO center at this level is established and continues NATO's presence in Norway

[2192] The further modernization of the Armed Forces in the period 2005–

[2193] Prerequisites for the realization of the structure Within the financial framework recommended in this proposition, a usable, modern and flexible defense adapted to the assigned tasks shall be developed

[2194] However, this requires that the prioritization principles described earlier are followed up in practice

[2195] Quality must be prioritized over quantity, and available departments must be prioritized over mobilization departments

[2196] The content of the units and their availability are more important than the number of units, and weapons, equipment and training standards are more important than the number of soldiers

[2197] This will provide an overall better Defence in relation to the security vehicle and the likely challenges and risks we face

[2198] This does not mean that quantity is without value

[2199] Quantity will, among other things, affect persistence, and there is a lower quantitative threshold for what elements in the structure are meaningful to continue

[2200] If this threshold is exceeded, it may be appropriate to remove the capacity completely, because it does not have the desired effect and is also a cost driver in that it necessitates the development of expertise and infrastructure

[2201] In such cases, it may be more appropriate to focus on other types of capacities, or on multinational cooperation

[2202] It is not appropriate to continue elements that there are no resources to modernize

[2203] However, continuing a larger structure than recommended in this proposition, for example by retaining extra mobilization forces as a reserve, will create a negative spiral effect, because resources are spent on elements that do not contribute to solving the Armed Forces' tasks in any case

[2204] This will in turn prevent the modernization of those units that are intended to have higher priority

[2205] In the long term, this will mean that the ambition of a modern, flexible and relevant defense will have to be abandoned

[2206] It is therefore better to invest in fewer units

[2207] If a dramatic security policy change were to occur in the future, making it necessary to increase the size and volume of the Armed Forces, such regeneration would have to be based on the technology and the requirements for competence, equipment and training and exercise levels that apply at that time

[2208] Retaining structural elements that are already, or are becoming, outdated, based on the desire for regeneration capacity, would therefore be highly inappropriate and constitute a misuse of the Armed Forces' total resources

[2209] Prioritizing quality is therefore a crucial structural measure also in a possible future regeneration perspective

[2210] The main goal of the further development of the Armed Forces is to ensure the ability to react quickly with the right type of capacity across the entire spectrum of the Armed Forces' tasks

[2211] The proposed structure contributes significantly in this direction, and will provide increased operational capability over the period, both to operate together with allies and to solve the tasks that the Armed Forces must be able to handle alone

[2212] The most likely tasks – peacetime tasks, national incident and crisis management and participation in multinational operations – are being carried out in a very satisfactory manner

[2213] The structure includes both elements with high responsiveness and elements with somewhat lower readiness, but the total volume of available units has increased significantly

[2214] An essential prerequisite for this increased capacity is the measures within the personnel area, described in Chapter 6, which will ensure a more appropriate age and competence profile as well as better utilization of the Armed Forces' personnel resources across the entire spectrum of tasks

[2215] The personnel area is critically important for the Armed Forces' operational capability

[2216] The quality reform in the Home Guard should be highlighted as an example of how, by prioritizing quality, implementing structural measures, and removing some of the unnecessary constraints and assumptions that have limited flexibility so far, accessibility and relevance in relation to the new tasks can be increased

[2217] In the new structure of the Home Guard, emphasis has been placed on dedicating a core of task forces that can be deployed where the need arises nationally, while other tasks are handled by reinforcement and follow-up forces

[2218] This provides a very good starting point for cost-effective resource utilization, and increased relevance in relation to the most likely tasks

[2219] The proposal for a new structure includes a number of deployable joint capabilities that are both central to supporting Norwegian forces, which can constitute independent Norwegian force contributions or contribute to increased protection for the rest of the structure

[2220] At the same time, several of the joint capacities, and the structure in general, have capacities that are highly relevant in support of tasks within societal security

[2221] The latter applies, for example, to the engineering, logistics, medical, military police and ARBC units

[2222] Strategic transport capacity is significantly strengthened through contracts with shipping companies for strategic maritime transport

[2223] During the period, strategic transport capacity will be further strengthened through multinational solutions

[2224] The changes in the direction of available and deployable forces have the greatest consequence for the 2003–

[2277] The further modernization of the Armed Forces in the period 2005–2008 is necessary, especially because this represents the most personnel-intensive branch of defense

[2278] The proposal for a new army structure provides a robust force pool, with high quality and responsiveness for all types of missions

[2279] In urgent crisis situations, a partially standing and flexible brigade can be used by Norwegian authorities at short notice

[2280] The most likely tasks within the prevailing security situation require an increased element of standing forces, and cannot be met with a larger mobilization structure

[2281] Norway's establishment of a deployable brigade is a historic boost for the Army, and will give us a qualitatively greater improved army

[2282] The brigade increases the range of capabilities Norway can offer the UN and NATO in all types of operations

[2283] It should be emphasized that the departments and personnel are given the competence to handle the entire spectrum of missions, including peacekeeping operations

[2284] The proposal for a new army structure is thus a crucial step in the development of a modern, usable and deployable army, which began with the establishment of the Telemark Battalion ten years ago

[2285] The army will have a somewhat limited ability to maintain ongoing engagement in foreign operations with the same type of capacity for an extended period of time with the brigade's battalions

[2286] Contributions to long-term peacekeeping operations outside Norway should in any case be rotated between different capacities and different branches of defence, instead of almost permanent engagement with the same type of capacity

[2287] NATO's concepts provide for such a rotation

[2288] It is important to distribute the burden and the increase in competence resulting from operations abroad across all branches of defense and most units, both to achieve a greater degree of predictability for families, to spread the development of competence, and for fair distribution between individuals and groups

[2289] Such a rotation is also appropriate given that the needs in, for example, a stabilization phase will change from contingent to contingent, as the operations in Kosovo and Afghanistan are examples of

[2290] At the same time, the Army's contribution to operations outside Norway must be seen in the context of tasks, preparedness and missions at home

[2291] In light of this, it is crucial that the Army and its force production model are organized in a way that provides the best possible operational capability

[2292] In light of this, a closer assessment of the organization and utilization of the Armed Forces' reserve forces will be carried out during the planning period

[2293] The establishment of the joint ISTAR unit means that Norway is at the forefront of NATO in this forward-looking area

[2294] UAV capacity integrated into ISTAR strengthens the ability to monitor and gather information

[2295] The ISTAR capacity will be a flexible unit, which, together with other forces from the defense branches, will be highly applicable in national incident and crisis management

[2296] For the Navy, the phasing in of modern vessels means a greatly improved operational capability, and will give Norway a very modern navy with an adapted logistics apparatus, which provides a significantly increased ability to secure Norwegian interests in the large sea areas, in addition to an increased ability to participate in overseas operations

[2297] The ability to lead national and multinational maritime forces is being further developed

[2298] Monitoring of Norwegian sea areas in the north is being improved through increased use of satellite information and further development of network solutions

[2299] New maritime helicopters will help increase the Coast Guard's capacity, and will also be a crucial part of the two-tier frigate-helicopter system

[2300] The upgrade of maritime surveillance aircraft also strengthens this surveillance capability

[2301] For the Air Force, priority is also given to

[2302] Upgrading of fighter aircraft to ensure that they meet the requirements of modern operations

[2303] Furthermore, the air defense is being upgraded to a more modern system better able to deal with the new threat

[2304] Summary The central premise in the design of the operational structure and activities is that the Armed Forces' capabilities must be adapted to the sum of the tasks in the new security landscape

[2305] Regardless of the resource level, this requires a changed alignment of the Armed Forces

[2306] The general requirements for military capability in a new era require modernization, innovation and flexible solutions

[2307] This is a development that applies regardless of our NATO membership, and is independent of participation in overseas operations

[2308] The adjustments to the operational structure recommended in this proposal, provided that the planned investments are implemented, will result in a significant improvement in quality and increase throughout the Armed Forces

[2309] This, seen in the context of the changes in personnel management, will strengthen the Armed Forces' relevance and effectiveness for national as well as international tasks

[2310] Training and practice

[2311] Priorities for training and exercise activities

[2312] The training activities must be adapted to new requirements and goals as a result of the restructuring of the Armed Forces 2003–

[2313] The further modernization of the Armed Forces in the period 2005–2008 and the introduction of the alliance's new command and force structure

[2316] When preparing the exercise program, strategically deployable capabilities with high response capability, as well as capabilities for national tasks and the management apparatus, are prioritized

[2317] It is crucial that the Armed Forces' operational structure is practiced in a realistic operational environment and within the organizational structures in which they are intended to be used

[2318] The purpose of training and exercise activities will, to a greater extent than previously, be to contribute to the transformation of the Armed Forces' military capabilities

[2319] The focus is on handling crisis situations, terrorist attacks and weapons of mass destruction in addition to more traditional tasks

[2320] Many of these tasks must be solved in the borderland between war and peace, and in peace-support operations outside Norway, they may also include law-related tasks

[2325] Strict balances will have to be made between training needs and available resources

[2359] Shooting and practice ranges

[2360] The Norwegian Armed Forces currently have and maintain an inventory of approximately 80 small and large land-based firing, training and regional ranges (SØR) across the country, with a total area of approximately 1,800 square kilometers

[2361] The vast majority of these are small, while a few fields cover large areas

[2362] In many cases, the land is rented, while owned land makes up about a quarter of the SØR areas

[2363] In connection with the ongoing modernization of Forsvaret, it is assumed that approximately half of the fields will be taken out of use within the next 8–10 years

[2364] Flexible and appropriate SØR fields located close to the military user are a clear prerequisite for good and effective soldier training with the aim of preparing Norwegian personnel for different types of missions

[2365] The armed forces are constantly developing through the supply of new materiel and new expertise

[2366] For large investments to yield dividends in the form of increased combat capability, it is crucial to be able to use the equipment in exercises that expose personnel to realistic situations in all forms of combat

[2367] Access to suitable shooting and practice ranges is key to this

[2368] At the same time, some of the SØR fields will provide Norwegian soldiers with good opportunities for timely, high-quality joint training with selected allied/foreign forces with whom we are expected to operate together both at home and abroad

[2369] Good training facilities are crucial to our ability to be attractive for allied training, including experimentation and concept development

[2370] In order to be able to integrate departments in the most realistic way possible and at a sufficiently high level, there is a need for several larger fields with adjacent low-flying areas

[2371] These must allow for the implementation of shooting exercises with heavier weapons in appropriate formations

[2372] They must also allow for realistic joint training with different departments and weapon types, either using live ammunition or simulator-based training systems

[2373] We will need a number of smaller practice ranges for practice weapons

[2374] It is an objective to make the force production of the Armed Forces' units cost-effective

[2375] Arrangements are made for proximity between shooting and training ranges and user departments, to make the ranges optimally accessible

[2376] The Home Guard will need a number of local shooting and practice ranges to ensure local training and exercises
